 It's not just age that matters, it turns out that the longer a patient has been on dialysis the less is their life expectancy after transplant (dialysis stresses the body so the sooner we get someone a transplant the better).Â  Although it may seem unfair, if we want to maximize total life expectancy we are doing the wrong thing by giving more points to patients who have been on the list longer.Â Â 
An optimized allocation system that took into account these considerations would increase total life
expectancy (modestly but significantly, about 11,500 extra life years) but it wouldn't benefit every individual.Â  Maximizing life expectancy would shift organs away from older people and people who have been on the waiting list a long time towards younger people.Â  As a result, some patients have argued that LYFT is unfair.Â  The Office of Civil Rights is even asking whether LYFT might violate age discrimination laws.Â Â 
But consider, would the older patients have objected to LYFT when they were younger?Â  If not, shouldn't their objections be discounted?Â  More formally, consider how people would vote behind a veil of ignorance.Â  By definition a LYFT approach maximizes total life expectancy, so without knowing the specifics of who you are or when you might need a transplant it's likely that behind a veil of ignorance just about everyone would favor LYFT.Â  Thus, in my view LYFT is a fair and ethical system.Â 
Here are previous MR posts on kidney transplant policy.
title: Optimizing Kidney Allocation: LYFT for LIFE

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Keep in mind that unemployment rates today are disproportionately concentrated in low-income and low-education workers.Â  Haven't we been told, for years, that these same individuals are seeing some mix of stagnant and eroding wages?Â  That they are experiencing downward mobility?Â  That the real value of health care benefits has been falling and that more and more jobs don't offer health care benefits at all?Â  
Doesn't that meanâ€¦umâ€¦their wages aren't so sticky downwards?Â  And thus Keynesian economics is not the final story?
Or take illegal immigrant Mexican construction workers, a group which lost jobs in large numbers following the crash.Â  Are they â€” who often came from $1 a day environments â€“Â also supposed to have sticky wages?Â  They are out of work in massive numbers.Â  A lot of them went back home, which is a sign they are willing to make major adjustments.Â  It simply may beÂ they were no longer employable in the United States at any plausible wage.
The alternative model is that many low-education workersÂ are not employable through marginal changes in current conditions.Â  It may require a bigÂ upward Schwung for the entire chain of labor, so that desperate employers at the bottom of the ladder, unable to find anyone else,Â grudgingly hire these not-so-productive individuals because there is no other way of expanding.Â  In other words, it requires conditions which raise the marginal value product of these workers to the private sector, keeping in mind that the fixed costs of hiring a worker mostly have been going up due to the greater bureaucratization of society.
Under this hypothesis, the stimulus that works in the short-run is direct government employment of low-skilled labor, not funneling money through private contracting, and hoping the unemployed get picked up.
What should the government do with these workers?Â  Does their direct employment conflict with the Davis-Bacon Act or other regulations?Â  What wage should we pay to make sure we don't drain off workers from private sector jobs?Â  How much longer does it take such forms of stimulus to result in sustainable, private sector jobs?
As you'll see in my Principles text with Alex, we both believe that wage stickiness (both nominal and real) is a genuine issue in market settings, even in the absence of government intervention.Â  Still, I'm not convinced stickiness is the major problem today, at least not in a simple, direct manner.
If there is going to be more U.S. stimulus, it's exact nature should be thought through very carefully.Â  It's an additional question whether ourÂ politics is up to that.
title: How sticky are wages today anyway?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Paris has dozens of restaurants which are better than any in Berlin, and then hundreds more better than the rest.Â  Yet it may be the case that you have, overall, a better food life in Berlin than in Paris.
Berlin has a weakÂ reputation among foodies, but culinary life in the cityÂ is much improved.Â  Here are my tips forÂ a good eating life in Berlin:
1. Find aÂ steady source of innovative rolls, buns,Â and dark breads.Â  These are the glories of Berlin and in many parts of town there will be at least one such source per residential block.Â  The more irregular the colors, seeds, and topologies of the breads, the more enthusiastically you should buy them.Â  Do not treat this as the French bread buying experience.
2. Find a source for good spreads, such as cherry, raspberry, etc. and stock up.Â  Repeatedly apply the spreadsÂ to the breads, until death of the researcherÂ intervenes.Â  This procedureÂ is the basis for everything else you will do.Â  It ensuresÂ that allÂ of your food days will beÂ good ones.
3. Seek out mid-level German restaurants, of the kind promoted in the Time Out Guide;Â Renger-Patzsch is a good example.Â  The vegetables in such places will be consistently excellent.
4. The speed and service quality of most meals will be much better if you arrive before 7 p.m.
5. Don't obsess over German food.Â  It's underrated, but stillÂ a lot of it isn't that good.Â  In Berlin, and many other parts of Germany, you have first-class delicatessens or stores with foodstuffs from France, Italy, and many other parts of the world.Â  Use them.Â  Berlin offers one of the best overall selections in this regard, better thanÂ New York City or Paris, for instance, in terms of real access.Â  You can eatÂ first-rate French cheese every day.
6. When it comes to Berlin German food, don't eat anything in a sauce.Â  It will be either boring or disgusting.Â  Sorry.
7. The sausage spread at the KaDeWe (make sure you live near that place) is probably the best in the entire world.Â  Go there regularly.Â  They also have first-rate sausages from France, Spain, and other countries, as well as an unparalleled selection of sausages from the different regions of Germany, organized one region per case.Â  This food source, like #1, insures that each of your food days will be a splendid one.
8. Go to Berlin's numerous and varied ethnic restaurants, especially in the slightly lower rent districts.Â  If the food is supposed to be spicy, you must repeat the following incantation several times: "Ich will es essen, genau wie Sie es zu Hause essen.Â  Ich bin kein deutscher."Â  [I wantÂ to eat it exactly as you eat it at home.Â  I am not a German."]Â  Repeat especially that last part: "Ich bin kein deutscher."Â  Repeat it even if you are a German.Â  This will usually work and typically your Chinese or Thai or Indian server will smile and laughÂ in response.Â  If they view you as a German, you are screwed no matter what.Â  Simply asking for the food to be "spicy" or even "very spicy" is laughable.Â  It is showing yourself to be a fool and a sucker.
9.Â Food here is much cheaper than in Paris, and it is much easier to get into virtually any restaurant.Â  Take advantage of both features.
10. Italian food here is almost always reasonably good, and reasonably cheap, but it is rarely great.Â  Lots of cream sauces.Â  It's a good enough fall back and you find it virtually everywhere.Â  A quite good pasta for $6 or even less is a common experience.Â  Sometimes it's actually German food in disguise, or not in disguise, such as when you get Carpaccio with Pfifferlinge.
11. For ethnic food, I recommendÂ the following: Tian Fu in Wilmersdorf (very good Sichuan), Suriya-Kanthi (Sri Lankan in Prenzlauer Berg),Â Genazvale (Georgian food in Charlottenburg), Degirman is one good Turkish place of many, a slew of authentic Mexican restaurantsÂ (more than in Virginia), DAO restaurant in Charlottenburg (Thai food, best papaya salad I've had, all-around excellent), and Schneeweiss has first-rateÂ Wiener Schnitzel.
Overall Sri Lankan and Nepalese and East bloc cuisines areÂ better here, or more available, than in the USA.
If you visit for one day, you won't be so impressed with culinary life in Berlin.Â  If you stay for a month, you won't want to go back to what you had before.
title: How to eat well in Berlin

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
One summary of the detailsÂ is hereÂ (I don't know whateverÂ inside story there may be), but the bottom line is that he had to resign from The Washington PostÂ because of negative comments he made about conservative figures on a supposedly private email list.Â  Weigel's job for the Post was to cover the conservative movement and it seems the Post expected him to maintain a more objective stance, includingÂ in his private emails.Â  Matt Yglesias has more extensive coverage of the episode and here is Ross Douthat.Â  Here is Weigel's account and apology, which includes the postings which got him into trouble.Â  And here is a detailed Politico article.
It isÂ likely I prefer Weigel over his replacement, and if you're wondering I don'tÂ know Weigel well, even though he lives nearby.
At a more general level this is a tax on journalists, who now have a greater fear of being fired for past actions.Â  It's also a tax on the moody, the volatile, the web-savvy, the non-mainstream, and a subsidy to in-control smooth talkers and careful writers.
The Washington Post wrote:

â€œBut weâ€™re living in an era when maybe we need to add a levelâ€� of inquiry, he [a WP web site managing editor] said. â€œIt may be in our interests to ask potential reporters: â€˜In privateâ€¦ have you expressed any opinions that would make it difficult for you to do your job.â€�

I'm not sure what kind of answers they expect to that question nor what they understand by the word "private" in that context.Â  
Conceptually, the core problem is that the distinction between the private and public spheres is breaking down, but at different rates for individuals and mainstream institutions.Â  The practical question is what an equilibrium would look like for the WP, given that the paper courts advertisers, relies on political contacts, and wishes to avoid becoming a target for right-wing (and left-wing) media.Â  It's easy to imagine the targets ofÂ Weigel's criticisms citing them repeatedly against the Washington Post and questioning the Post's objectivity.Â  "Oh, that was written by the guy who said thatâ€¦"
One possible outcome is that the current public code of behaviorÂ becomes applied to writers' private lives and I suppose that is what we are seeing and it is also what a lot of "common knowledge" models would predict.Â  That is, most of us know thatÂ many writers say such things in private, but that's tolerated as long as it doesn't become common knowledgeÂ about any particular writer.
Common knowledge mechanisms often lead toÂ inefficient (and unfair) outcomes, in partÂ by non-convexying returns with regard to the actions of the individual.Â  Maybe we would like taxes to be linked to individual type, but common knowledge mechanisms tend to link the actual "tax" to how social forces process information about an individual.Â  A polemicist who is secretly taped encounters a greatly different outcome.than a polemicist who is not taped.
One option is for public institutions to adopt aÂ "statute of limitations" for private remarks and with a short time window.Â  That would not help in this case, since Weigel's relevant postings do not predate his Post employment; still it might be a good reform.Â Â Another option is for public institutions to adopt different norms for their web writers.Â  There are already different norms to some extent (web writings receive less editing, for instance), but it is hard to spread the different norm for the writing to become a different norm for the writer.Â  Web traffic is already massive for newspapers, and most readers probably do not distinguish between different kinds of paper employees, such as web vs. non-web.Â  Anyway, it's a fuzzy line if a writer has both web and non-web output.
A more radical change would move away from the manufactured image ofÂ the objective newspaper, but this isÂ especially difficultÂ for the Post, given that it relies on both conservative and liberal sources for its key political coverage.
Overall, we need more incentive-compatible, generalizableÂ organizational reforms which will allow mainstreamÂ institutionsÂ to have more flexible relationships, and indeed sometimes more distanced relationships,Â with their writers.Â  Yet reputational forces are often quite blunt, and grossly calculated, and mainstream institutions areÂ not very far along on making such reforms work.
title: The Dave Weigel resignation

Here is my latest NYT column, which they titled "The Pendulum Swings Back to Austerity."Â  Excerpt:

The unfolding of the financial crisis has also changed the publicâ€™s sense of where change is needed, both in the United States and Europe. The tragedies of 2008 were represented by Bear StearnsÂ and Lehman Brothers â€“ both private-sector institutions. In 2010, the financial crisis has spread to sovereign debt, with Greece as the most obvious example. 
All of these developments are part of one broader story of overreach and complacency. Yet the 2008 crises were attached more directly to market institutions, while the 2010 crises are more closely linked to governments. Because politicians and voters are more influenced by the latest developments than by news from two or three years earlier, a cautious attitude toward public-sector spending has been further cemented. 

And this:

Democracies, like markets, have some self-correcting mechanisms, and we are now seeing those at work in the United States and many European countries. (Spain and Britain, for example, are pursuing fiscal austerity aggressively.) 
The lessons are straightforward. First, to paraphrase the French moralist La Rochefoucauld, things are never as good, or as bad, as they seem. Second, the Obama reforms, like the Reagan revolution, are turning out to be radically incomplete, which should come as no surprise. 
Finally, effective political ideas are those that can still do good in half-baked form. We have neglected this insight in designing financial reform, and it remains to be seen if we can apply it successfully to climate change. 

Overall, I believe we are headed toward slower growth and a larger public sector, but I do not believe we are headed down the road to serfdom.Â  At the same time, I am aiming at a different target.Â  Critics of incrementalism are usually too focused on the single issue at hand â€” where they are sure they know best â€” and not sufficiently aware of the efficiency properties of the broader system, which introduces self-correction mechanisms to counter or limit most major changes.

Brad DeLong discusses a recent short essay by Kartik Athreya; Matt Yglesias chips in, as does Scott Sumner.
My view is a little different than Brad's.Â  I would say that economics is really, really, really, really, really, really, really hard.Â  And that's leaving out a few of theÂ "reallys."
It's so hard that experts don't always do it well.Â Â The expertsÂ are constantly prone to correction by non-experts, by practitioners, by people who are self-educated economic experts but not professional economists, and by people who know some economics and a lot about some other field(s).Â  It is very often that we â€” at least some of us â€“Â are wrong and at least some of those other people are right.Â  Furthermore those other people are often more meta-rational than a lot of professional economists.
Even very simple problems can be quite hard, such as why nominal wages are sometimes sticky or why particular markets don't always clear, in the absence of legal impediment.Â  Why doesn't the restaurant charge more on a Saturday night?Â  You can imagine how hard the hard problems are, such as what level of public expenditure is consistent with an ongoing and workableÂ democratic equilibrium.
Putting aside agreement and ideology, and just focusing on how one understands an issue, I'll take my favorite non-Ph.d. bloggers over most professional economists, six out of seven days a week.Â Â Not to estimate a coefficient, but to judge public policy, thereby integrating and evaluating broad bodies of knowledge?Â  It's not even close.

In advance of July 4, Patri Friedman and co-bloggers are discussing secession (remember, we call it the American revolution they call it secession) at Let a Thousand Nations Bloom. Â Here is Patri on secession as a startup:Â 
America did not merely secede and copy the governing documents or style of the United Kingdom. Rather, it innovated, creating a system based on the English Common Law, yet different, one with explicit checks and balances to restrain government, and with no place for a monarch. It was an experiment with a more radical form of democracy than existed anywhere in the 18th-century world.


	And it was an incredibly successful experiment, as the combination of that innovative rule-set and the empty frontier resulted in America growing rapidly in population, wealth, and influence. During the open immigration periods of the 19th century, some years saw over a million new immigrants arrive â€œyearning to breathe freeâ€�. As a result, the new American state had influence far beyond its shores.


	This influence occured in two major ways. First, America served as a test of the brand-new American Constitution, and the Founding Fathersâ€™ philosophy about the role of government. By showing that it worked well in practice, political philosophers, politicians, voters, and revolutionaries around the world were (slowly) convinced that this was the best government technology to be had. Second, America dramatically outcompeted existing states, based on the simple metric of net migration. Those million+ people a year who went to America can be thought of as customers of government services voting with their feet, which means that other countries were losing market share.


	You may not be used to thinking of government in this sort of economic and business framework, but it is a core part of our philosophy here at Let A Thousand Nations Bloom, and we find it provides a unique and refreshing angle on government. In this case, it shows us the invisible, long-term effects of the American Revolution.

There was an unusual match between Barbados and Grenada.
Grenada went into the match with a superior goal difference, meaning that Barbados needed to win by two goals to progress to the finals. The trouble was caused by two things. First, unlike most group stages in football competitions, the organizers had deemed that all games must have a winner. All games drawn over 90 minutes would go to sudden death extra time. Secondly and most importantly, there was an unusual rule which stated that in the event of a game going to sudden death extra time the goal would count double, meaning that the winner would be awarded a two goal victory.
Barbados was leading 2-0 until the 83rd minute, when Grenada scored, making it 2-1. Approaching the dying moments, the Barbadians realized they had no chance of scoring past Grenada's mass defense, so they deliberately scored an own goal to tie the game at 2-2. This would send the game into extra time and give them another half hour to break down the defense. The Grenadians realized what was happening and attempted to score an own goal as well, which would put Barbados back in front by one goal and would eliminate Barbados from the competition.
However, the Barbados players started defending their opposition's goal to prevent them from doing this, and during the game's last five minutes, the fans were treated to the incredible sight of Grenada trying to score in either goal. Barbados also defended both ends of the pitch, and held off Grenada for the final five minutes, sending the game into extra time. In extra time, Barbados notched the game-winner, and, according to the rules, was awarded a 4-2 victory, which put them through to the next round.

The full story is here and I thank Solomon Gold for the pointer.Â  Angus also blogged this story, with video evidence as well.

Paul, a loyal MR reader,Â writes to me and queries:

â€¦would or should knowing that someone is deeply religious affect your assessment of the reliability of their economic judgments? I used to think not, but in the last couple of years have been gradually changing my mind. The financial crisis has brought out how many serious macro and micro misjudgments were due in part to the unwillingness of economists to re-examine cherished foundational beliefs. I now view with even greater suspicion than before any adherence to the idea that faith provides a justification for ignoring logic and evidence. But the paradox is that I have no actual evidence that religious economists were more likely than secular ones to cling to foundational economic hypotheses in the face of considerations that should have led them to change their minds. It is even imaginable that they were less likely to do so, since secular economists might have exercised similar failures of reasoning about non-theological issues. That is, antipathy to metaphysical reason might be a substitute for antipathy to economic reason, instead of being a complement as I have been presuming. Can anyone provide anecdotal or statistical evidence on this? 

I don't know of any systematic evidence, but oftenÂ I favor portfolio models of dogmatism (by the way, don't argue in the comments about whether religion is necessarily dogmatism; that's not the relevant point here and I'll delete discussion of that.Â  If you wish just treat this as a discussion of dogmatism).
That is, most people haveÂ an internal psychological need to fulfill a "quota of dogmatism."Â  If you're very dogmatic in one area, you may be less dogmatic in others.Â  I've also met people â€” I won't name names â€” who are extremely dogmatic on ethical issues but quite open-minded on empirics.Â  The ethical dogmatism frees them up to follow the evidence on the empirics, as they don't feel their overall beliefs are threatened by the empirical results.
Some people, if they feel they must always follow the evidence, respond by skewing their interpretation of that evidence.
There's a lesson here.Â  If you wish to be a more open-minded thinker, adhere to some extreme and perhaps unreasonableÂ fandoms, the more firmly believed the better and the more obscure the area the better.Â  This will help fulfill your dogmatism quota, yet without much skewing your more important beliefs.
An alternative view is that people become addicted to dogmatism and the dogmatic habits spread to many more realms of their thought.Â  I believe this alternative model is true above some margin of dogmatism and also if the dogmatism infects the "wrong areas of thought."
I would like to know more about what the dogmatism portfolio looks like and what are the relevant coefficients of substitution and complementarity.
I believe in portfolio models of dogmatism very very strongly.Â

There are many commentaries on David Leonhardt's article today on whether we should be raising taxes and cutting government spending, as was done in 1937.Â  Yet I don't see anyone â€” at least not today â€” talking about monetary policy during 1936-7.Â  A bit earlier, David Beckworth stepped up to the plate:

Is the Federal Reserve (Fed) making a similar mistake to the one it made in 1936-1937? If you recall, the Fed during this time doubled the required reserve ratio under the mistaken belief that it would reign in what appeared to be an inordinate buildup of excess reserves. The Fed was concerned these funds could lead to excessive credit growth in the future and decided to act preemptively. author: Tyler Cowen
text:
In the whole discussion about whether the U.S. should borrow more now when the interest rates are low, I miss one crucial thing â€“ what happens when the debt comes due?
Risk-free debt is really risk-free only when the maturity also coincides with terminal repayment. But assume that the U.S. borrows an extra trillion of dollars now, due in 10 years (the average debt duration of the U.S. debt is something like 4 years?). Sure, the interest rate is low, but the borrowing is cheap only as long as we assume that during the 10 years the U.S. repays this whole extra debt, compared to what would have happened in the baseline world.
If not, the U.S. will need to refinance this debt in 10 years, and potentially at much higher interest rates. There is a potentially very large risk looming. Greece has experienced this the hard way â€“ it collapsed not because it necessarily needed new borrowing but because it had to roll over the old borrowing at impossibly high rates.
And I have not heard the advocates of more borrowing to suggest any credible offsetting mechanism that would lead to repayment (not replacement with other borrowing) of this extra debt at or before maturity. But then the idea "let's borrow now because it's cheap" becomes seriously flawed.
I would compare those who advocate such outright borrowing without committing to credibly repay at maturity to people who fall for teaser mortgage rates and are rather negatively surprised to see the rate adjust later. It is interesting though that there seems to be a large positive correlation between people who advocate government borrowing because rates are low NOW, and those who call for protecting consumers against reckless lenders who tease them with a low temporary rate. To quote a famous Canadian singer, Isn't it ironic?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Take this one with a grain of salt, but here is the latest:

Kennedy's breakthrough, published in the journal Apeiron this week, is based on stichometry: the measure of ancient texts by standard line lengths. Kennedy used a computer to restore the most accurate contemporary versions of Plato's manuscripts to their original form, which would consist of lines of 35 characters, with no spaces or punctuation. What he found was that within a margin of error of just one or two percent, many of Plato's dialogues had line lengths based on round multiples of twelve hundred.
The Apology has 1,200 lines; the Protagoras, Cratylus, Philebus and Symposium each have 2,400 lines; the Gorgias 3,600; the Republic 12,200; and the Laws 14,400.
Kennedy argues that this is no accident. "We know that scribes were paid by the number of lines, library catalogues had the total number of lines, so everyone was counting lines," he said. He believes that Plato was organising his texts according to a 12-note musical scale, attributed to Pythagoras, which he certainly knew about.

Do note this:

Kennedy believes his findings restore what was the standard, mainstream view which held for 2,000 years "from the first generation of Plato's followers, up through the renaissance". This held that "he wrote symbolically and that if you worked hard and became wise you could understand the symbols and penetrate his text to his underlying philosophy." Only in the last few hundred years has an emphasis on the literal meanings of texts led to a neglect of their figurative meanings.
It also explains why it is that Aristotle, Plato's pupil, emphatically claimed that Plato was a follower of Pythagoras, to the bafflement of most contemporary scholars.

I used to consider allegiance to this idea (Montaigne, also, for symbolic codes) as one of my absurd beliefs, but maybe now it is looking better.Â  I will have to look elsewhere.
title: Are there hidden codes in Plato?

author: Alex Tabarrok
text:
The most obvious way in which sticky wages impede employment is by keeping the cost of hiring workers above the equilibrium wage. The standard story explains that sticky wages increase unemployment. The standard story, however, is not the only and perhaps not the most important transmission mechanism.
Wages are the largest component of costs thus sticky wages keep costs high and profits low. Â The point is obvious once stated but it has implications for how we look at sticky wages. Â Tyler, for example, writes:

	[Consider] illegal immigrant Mexican construction workers, a group which lost jobs in large numbers following the crash. Are they â€” who often came from $1 a day environments â€” also supposed to have sticky wages? They are out of work in massive numbers.
The focus here is on the unemployed workers with the argument implicit thatÂ it's the stickiness of their wages which counts (which makes sense given the standard story). Â But suppose that the problem is that firms can't get capital to expandâ€“perhaps because the banking system is not working wellâ€“then what matters for firm expansion is free cash flow. Â But sticky wages keep firm costs high, reducing free cash flow and inhibiting expansion. In this argument,Â the stickiness that matters is the sticky wages of the employed workers.
A story which focuses on employed workers has several advantages. Â First, the wages of employed workers are clearly more sticky than the wages of unemployed workersâ€“in fact, if you are employedÂ real wages are up slightly. Moreover, since more than 90% of workers are employed this type of argument has leverage. Â 
If there are fixed costs, new firms do not arise instantly soÂ infra-marginal sticky wages can be important forÂ a number of "balance-sheet" reasons in addition but related to the free cash flow story such as debt constraints or various coordination and risk reasons. Â
title: Sticky wage transmission mechanisms

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Brad DeLong asks:

When would it be time to judge the Irish experiment in preemptive fiscal austerity to be a failure, Tyler?

The immediateÂ question is whether Ireland had a choice in the first place.Â  When it comes to total external debt, private plus public, Ireland is in one of the most desperate situations.Â  (Be careful, though, some published figures include financial institutions to which the Irish government has no real liability and thus overstate Irish external debt by quite a bit).Â  Ireland doesn't have the same flexibilityÂ as do Germany and the United States, nothing close to that.Â  Read this article for an estimate of the change in primary fiscal balance required for Ireland; it's scary and doesn't indicate a lot of flexibility, which supports the conventional wisdom on Ireland,Â from the OECD, the European Commission,Â from Ireland itself, and arguably you addÂ the IMF to that list as well.Â  
Furthermore, Ireland as a small, open economyÂ experiences a relatively high degree of fiscal leakage.
By the way, you shouldn't simply assume that the initial fifteen plunge in gdp was due to fiscal caution; Ireland was after Iceland perhaps the most overextended country in the crisis.
Here's a Morgan Stanley analysis of Ireland, which basically suggests "it's complicated."Â  It also suggests a reasonable chanceÂ the current strategy will work out OK.Â  It is complicated, andÂ the mere factÂ that spending is a component ofÂ national income accounts doesn't mean that more spending is always a good thing.Â 
Ireland in factÂ has done a negative fiscal stimulus.Â  Earlier, Ireland madeÂ the mistake of joining the Eurozone.Â  See also this study of Ireland, 1987-89, an earlier decisive and successful fiscal adjustment, in the days of the Irish Punt.Â  The Euro today makes matters harder for Ireland, yet that doesn't imply they have greater license to spend today, in fact it canÂ imply the contrary.
Paul Krugman pointed out that the fiscally tighter Ireland did not have a better CDS price than the more wishy-washy Spain.Â  Yet Ireland has a bigger external debt problem, may be less protected by "too big to fail," is a smaller nation, and has less control over its destiny; the (roughly) equal price may reflect what is a superior Irish effort.Â  In any case, Spain is hardly a walking advertisement for not going the Irish route.
The Irish also hope that whatever output they "leave on the table" today, they can make up with Solow catch-up growth.
If you would like to read a brief on behalf of Irish stimulus, try this.Â  The author admits that Ireland would have to significantly raise corporate taxes, a former linchpin of its growth (whether you think that efficiency-enhancing or international rent-seeking, it is still true).Â  Is it worth it?Â  How much would such a policy damage Irish growth and credibility?
Kevin O'Rourke also has good but scattered writings onÂ the topicÂ of Irish stimulus.Â  His first preference is greater fiscal federalism within the EU.Â  Last month he also wrote that, lacking such a reform,Â Ireland had no choice.
This June, Irish consumer confidence hit a three-year high.Â  Here's one estimate that wages have been falling four to five percent a year, and will continue to fall, plus the Euro has been falling.Â  You could argue there has already been an adjustment in the twenty-five percent range.Â  None of that is proof of recovery, but there are some green shoots.Â  Here is the very latest report, indicating that economic growth may be resuming; admittedly it's just a forecast from the government.Â  Exports are showingÂ growth and retail sales are rising slightly.
The Irish Times reports today: "For the first time in three years, there are now more reasons for hope than for despair.Â  This week a raft of indicators, when taken together, give grounds to believe that the foundations of a jobs-generating recovery are falling into place."
Do interpret that with extreme caution.Â  For various debates, follow The Irish Economy blog, including in the comments.
On these critical questions,Â in the pro-stimulus for Ireland posts, IÂ don't see a level of detail which would rebut these quite mainstream, not-emanating-from-the-gamma-quadrantÂ opinions â€” that the Irish did more or less the right thing in a very unpleasant situation.Â  
The Irish experiment remains an open book.Â  In the meantime,Â it's simply not true that the pre-emptive austerity advocates are committing some kind of economic malpractice.Â  Three years out from now, let's compare Ireland to the other PIIGS.
title: When will we know if Irish pre-emptive fiscal austerity is a failure?

There has been much recent discussion of the topic and I apologize (to RA, among others) for being late to the party.Â  Here is one piece by Yves Smith in the NYTÂ and here is an Economist symposium on the topic, with many first-rate contributors.Â  Overall I am puzzled at the nature of theÂ worry here.Â  Corporations with cash surpluses are not destroying real resources, nor are they stuffing cash in their mattresses.Â  They are investing in financial assets.
Take a financiallyÂ conservative corporation, which holds its surplus in the form of T-Bills.Â  If it bought the T-Bills fresh at auction, that's lending money out to the government and the capital is still deployed.Â  Isn't that calledâ€¦in some circlesâ€¦stimulus?Â  (I've even heard the multiplier might be 1.4!Â  Or does only the borrower get credit and not the lender?)Â  It's trickier if the corporation buys the T-Bill on the secondary market, but still a) someone else has the money now, and b) this resale opportunity encourages other investorsÂ to buy freshly created T-Bills, thus putting capital in the hands of the government.Â  In terms of final effect, there should be a near-equivalence between buying old and new T-Bills.
Of course you might think the government is not spending this money well, but that's the problem of the government, not the corporate surpluses, which indeed are being invested.Â  I ran a surplus this last year and paid off some of my mortgage; does anyone think I destroyedÂ net real resource investment?Â  (In fact I redistributed profits away from the financial sector, I suspect, which isÂ goodÂ for the real economy at this point.)
If velocity is too slow for a social optimum, is it the corporations â€” who strive to rapidly invest excess cash in the till â€” who are at fault?Â  Even if corporations are not helping matters, are they doing anything worse than passing off a hot potato?
You might make an external cost argument.Â  Perhaps each corporation does well by holding T-Bills, but the system as a whole suffers under the encroachment of state power and public sector expansion.Â  That's not an argument which many proponentsâ€¦.do I even need to finish this sentence?Â Â 
It is perfectly fine to claim that we have aÂ sectoral misallocation and that high corporate cash reserves are a symptom of this problem, for instance maybe there is too much lending toÂ the safer, commercial paper-issuingÂ big corporations and not enoughÂ lending for higher-yielding, riskier start-ups (no one knows which risks to take), or whichever story you wish to tell.Â  I hold a version of that view myself, but it's very different from believing that high cash reserves are stifling investment per se.
By the way, these high cash reserves are one reason why I don't think Alex's nominal wage stickiness story explains current unemployment.
Why is it so frequent that economists take Keynes's analysis of sitting on currency and apply it to savings and investment?
File under "Yet another discussion of the Junker problem."
title: Why are corporations saving so much?

I don't know and neither does anybody else.Â  Here is one set of recent estimates, as reported in The Guardian:

In a bleak assessment, entitled "quantifying the unthinkable", they warn that in the first year alone, so by the start of 2012, output would fall between 5% and 9% across various member states, while their new national currencies would fall by 50%.

Please don't fix those numbers in your mind, soÂ here's the real point.Â  The new national currencies, of the poorer countries, would fall by some amount.Â  If that amount is small, that also provides reason to believe the current Eurozone can survive.Â  If that amount is large, it provides reason to believe the current Eurozone cannot survive.Â  (The poorer countries would now have to deflate a lot, and there would beÂ a greater risk of a speculative attack on their banking systems.)
You might think that the collapse of the current Eurozone, and the devaluations, areÂ good in the longer run (I do), but in the short runÂ the entire processÂ would be a nasty, volatility-laden, solvency-revaluingÂ shock to the entire global economy.
You therefore should expect "either an OK outcome, or a very nasty shock," in exactly that conjunctive form.Â  You shouldn't expect something in between.Â  The conditions where the current Eurozone collapses are precisely the same conditions where the shock of transition is a big one.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
A few of my lunch compadres have asked why I compare cryonics (unfavorably)Â to acts of charity, rather than comparing other acts of personal consumption (I enjoy the gelato here in Berlin) to charity.Â  My view is this: the decision to have one's head frozen is not primarily instrumental but rather expressive.Â  Look at the skewed demographics of the people who do it, namely highly intelligent male readers of science fiction, often with tech jobs.Â  Is it that they love their lives especially much?Â  Unlikely.Â  Instead it's a chance to stand for something and in a way which sets them apart from many others.Â Â It's a chance to stand for instrumental rationality, for Science, for attitudes which go beyond traditional religion, for the conquering of limits, for probabilistic reasoning, and for the notion that the subject sees hidden possibilities and resourcesÂ which more traditional observersÂ do not.
It's like voting for a very unusual political candidate.
In my view the people interested in cryonics are often highly meritorious, as is Robin.Â  So I'm very sympathetic with a) letting them do what they want, and b) praising them and their affiliations, simply because they are productive and smart and also not harming others.Â  Those factors militate in favor of cryonics and indeed I am happy to endorseÂ laissez-faire for the practice but still I don'tÂ find myself settling into really liking the idea.
Let's say I use another Hansonian construct and put everyone behind a contractarian veil of ignorance.Â  I then ask: given that we don't know who will be born into which position, which expressive symbols do we want these highly intelligent individuals to send, and also to identify with, given that reputation is limited and publicity is scarce?Â  Keep also in mind that society is insufficiently appreciative of intelligence and we would prefer that more people hadÂ greater respect for analytic thinking.Â  There are also many worthy causes out there.
I don't see the positive deal here.Â  I believe the world would be better off, and the relative status of the virtuous nerds higher,Â if instead the cryonics customers sent more signals which were perceived as running contrary to type.Â  IgnoringÂ cryonics, and promotingÂ charity,Â would do more to raise the status of intelligence and analytical thinking than does cryonics.
On the practical side,Â while I am a non-believer, I also think that charity has a greater chance of bringing a longer life to one's self â€“Â or immortality â€” than does signing a cryonics contract.Â  That's an even stronger triumph for probabilistic thinking than what the cryonics customers have on tap.

Kathleen Kahle, a professor at the University of Georgia's business school, offers another reason: the growth of high-tech companies, which tend to hold lots of cash. It is often suggested that Economics is a good major for individuals interested in becoming business leaders. Despite this widespread assertion, little research has been conducted on this topic. Ian Ayres writesÂ (source, with further explanation, here):

In our risk-reducing implementation, we want people to borrow to invest more when young and then invest less when older. The lifetime exposure to stocks is held constant. Compare the following two investment paths: 
Option 1 
Year 1 Invest $1 
Year 2 Invest $2 
Year 3 Invest $3 
Option 2 
Year 1 Invest $2 
Year 2 Invest $2 
Year 3 Invest $2 
Our view is that option 2 is the safer bet. 

That is a simple comparison, but I am still puzzled.Â  
First, under option one, the investor faces more price risk, given that share prices will move between period two and period three.Â  But price risk is not quantity risk, and a traditionally risk-averse investor, in the Arrow-Pratt sense, need not mind price risk on net.Â  If you tell me I can buy into Microsoft at p = 50, or accept a lottery with 0.5 (p = 100), 0.5 (p = 0), I might prefer the latter, noting that we live in an equity premium scenario and sometimes share price understates fundamental value.Â Â 
Second, under option one the investor buys less equity in the first period.Â  Let's assume that same investor holds T-Bills instead, or perhaps avoids debt.Â  There is nothing in the so-called "mutual fund theorem" which tells us what the T-Bills/equity ratio should be.Â  Maybe Ayres and Nalbuff think it should be higher â€” and maybe they're right â€” but that's an argument distinct from the "smoothing purchases over time" argument.
Is there a "smoothing equity purchases over time" argument which does not collapse into the "it's better to have a longer total exposure to the market" argument?Â  Or not?Â  Do Ayres and Nalebuff think it is OK if the "smoothing" argument boils down to an "there is actually an equity premium, so seek greater total market exposure over time" argument. (For instance, what if option one is the non-smoothed, but highly exposedÂ sequence "3, 2, 1" instead of the specifiedÂ non-smoothed but lesser exposed "1, 2, 3"?
I am very willing to admit that the confusion hereÂ isÂ mine, but confused I am.Â  Here is my previous post on the book.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
I am happy to see Paul Krugman address the question.Â  He writes:
So why not forget about open-market operations, and just drop the stuff
from helicopters? Well, remember that at this point cash and short-term
bonds are equivalent. So a helicopter drop is just like a temporary
lump-sum tax cut. And we would expect people to save much or most of
such a tax cut â€“ all of it, if you believe in full Ricardian
equivalence.

I hold a different opinion for two reasons.Â  First, cash and short-term bonds may be near-substitutes but they are not literally, strictly equivalent.Â  The nominal rate on T-bills is not exactly zero and furthermore you can't use a T-bill for every retail purchase.Â  The demand curve for real cash need slope down only slightly for a quantity theory result to hold.Â  After everyone spends the new cash balances, and prices rise, people end up with the quantity of real balances which they initially desired.Â  These equilibria have "knife-edge" properties, where "identical to T-Bills" and "nearly identical to T-Bills" do not bring the same results.Â  Tsiang showed this in a very good JMCB article on Friedman's optimum quantity of money, in the early 1970s and you might regard it as implicit in Bewley's Econometrica article on Friedman.
Second, after a helicopter drop no one need expect future taxes to be raised to retire the money (although maybe a sufficiently credible government could create such an expectation).Â  So there is no Ricardian motive to save the new cash, as Brad DeLong points out.Â  Indeed, if you think there is some chance that others will spend the money, raising the price level, you will want to spend your new cash soon, so as to preserve its value against forthcoming price inflation.Â  The resulting game-theoretic equilibrium, applying dominant strategies, again leads to higher prices, higher aggregate demand, and the desired quantity of real cash balances held.
Those are not the only possible cases (see the work of Fischer Black) but I take them to be the most sensible default cases.Â  Both indicate that a helicopter drop of cash will work fine in boosting aggregate demand.
The most likely scenario for no positive AD effect is simply that the helicopter drop is so small that no one expects a price level rise and thus no one expects an inflationary tax on the new cash, people (for bounded rationality reasons) treat the new cash as a transfer purely to themselves, the precautionary motive for saving is strong, and so the new money is simply held.Â  A larger helicopter drop should overcome that inertia, if need be.
Maybe these arguments are incorrect but they date from a consensus established in the mid- to late 1960s and early 1970s, much of it springing from Patinkin's book on money and the subsequent discussions thereof.Â  Krugman suggests this perspective is wrong, but he hasn't yet given me â€” or others â€” a reason to budge from it.

The world has reached gender parity in schooling and in a few years we will see a schooling ratio in favor of women.Â  Using UNESCO statistics (more detail here) on school life expectancy, the average country has a parity level of 1.01 in favor of women or, weighting by population, .991.Â  In other words, at current rates women can be expected to get the same number of years of education as men, as a world average.
Equal life expectancy of schooling on a world level does not mean that all is well â€“ basically we have a relatively small number of countries in which women get much less education than men and a large number of countries in which women get somewhat more education than men.Â  On the vertical axis in the figure below (click to enlarge) is total life expectancy in school and on the horizontal axis the ratio of female to male life expectancy in school.Â  The figure tells us a number of interesting things.Â  First, the largest imbalances are against women and these tend to occur in countries with a low level of total education.Â  South Korea is an interesting outlier.
Second, in India parity is below 1 and in China it is above 1.Â  In India female school life expectancy increased by a huge 2.5 years between 2000 and 2007 and the parity ratio increased from .77 to .9 so we can expect the (weighted) world parity level to easily tip over 1 in the next few years (if it has not done so already). The graph suggests that a ratio around 1.09 is the "norm" towards which countries are trending with development.
Interestingly, some of the Muslim countries, such as Pakistan and Afghanistan (no data for 2007-2008 but in 2004 the parity ratio was less than 0.5), are below parity but Qatar and Iran have some of the highest ratios in the world, both above US levels.
title: Gender Parity in Schooling Around the World

E. Barandiaran writes in the comments:

Tyler, I hope that tomorrow (7/14) you read this comment about Arnold Kling's challenge to BC: define money that meets two requirements. Please tell AK that his two requirements were the same that Milton F. argued for the QT of M to make sense â€“but as anyone familiar with the history of Milton's version knows, he failed miserably. I'm still waiting your definition of money.

Arnold Kling writes:

So my challenge for Bryan (and for the rest of the profession, because I am the one who is out on a limb on this) is to come up with a definition of money that satisfies two criteria. First, your monetary aggregate is correlated with nominal GDP in a reliable way (with "reliable" including that if you were to target it, the relationship would not fall apart). Second, the Fed controls that monetary aggregate reasonably closely.

No definition of money fits Arnold's challenge (though Bryan argues for the monetary base)Â and I'm not going to offer a single definition of money, period.Â  I see money first as a medium of account and then as an option on purchasing goods and services.Â  As an option,Â "money" is more likeÂ "credit cards" than many economists might find comfortable, but so be it.Â Â No single number very well summarizes the quantity or outstanding value of the money supply, properly understood to include the option value of lines of credit but also the option value of currency and bank reserves.Â  (Bill Barnett promotesÂ "divisia indices," which I view as a nice try to a hard-to-solve problem.)
That said,Â a large,Â exogenous shift in the money supplyÂ will raise the general level of prices.Â  There is overwhelming evidence for that proposition (check out my macro Principles text with Alex, for one good chart, or visit Zimbabwe).Â  If some mix of currency, bank reserves, and useful lines of credit go up, prices will go up too, in very rough proportion, no matter what the exact measure of the money supply should be.
A lot of the better criticisms of the quantity theory play off of whether "money" is exogenous in the first place.Â  Many of the points of these critics are well-taken, but still a properly specified exogenous boost in the money supply will bringÂ the traditional quantity theory result.Â  You just don't have to see that exogenous shift as the only relevant scenario for all real world monetary economics.
I see this post as "a lot of words."Â  I'm not saying much, I am just trying to limit how much other people's words confuse you.
On the quantity theory, I recommend reading and studying Arthur Marget'sÂ A Theory of Prices, especially volume II.Â  Marget was a penetratingÂ thinker who understood his chosen topics better than anyone else and who was very good at pulling out the deep truths in apparently simple propositions.Â  I think of him as the Scott Sumner of his day, minus a blog.
title: How should we define money? (warning: this post is pure semantics)

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
At a theme park, Gneezy conducted a massive study of over 113,000 people who had to choose whether to buy a photo of themselves on a roller coaster. They were given one of four pricing plans. Under the basic one, when they were asked to pay a flat fee of $12.95 for the photo, only 0.5% of them did so.
When they could pay what they wanted, sales skyrocketed and 8.4% took a photo, almost 17 times more than before. But on average, the tight-fisted customers paid a measly $0.92 for the photo, which barely covered the cost of printing and actively selling one. Thatâ€™s not the best business model â€“ the company proves itself to be generous, itâ€™s products sell like (free) hot-cakes, but its profit margins take a big hit. You could argue that Radiohead experienced the same thing â€“ their album was a hit but customers paid relatively little for it.
When Gneezy told customers that half of the $12.95 price tag would go to charity, only 0.57% riders bought a photo â€“ a pathetic increase over the standard price plan. This is akin to the practices of â€œcorporate social responsibilityâ€� that many companies practice, where they try to demonstrate a sense of social consciousness. But financially, this approach had minimal benefits. It led to more sales, but once you take away the amount given to charity, the sound of hollow coffers came ringing out. You see the same thing on eBay. If people say that 10% of their earnings go to charity, their items only sell for around 2% more.
But when customers could pay what they wanted in the knowledge that half of that would go to charity, sales and profits went through the roof. Around 4.5% of the customers asked for a photo (up 9 times from the standard price plan), and on average, each one paid $5.33 for the privilege. Even after taking away the charitable donations, that still left Gneezy with a decent profit.

The full article is here and I thank Michelle Dawson for the pointer.
title: â€œShared social responsibilityâ€� as a path to greater profit?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
So says Larry Kotlikoff, in his new book, entitled Jimmy Stewart is Dead: Ending the World's Ongoing Financial Plague with Limited Purpose Banking.Â  It'sÂ lively and polemic, and suddenly it lurches into a proposal to reform financial intermediation:

Under limited purposes banking the banks are themselves simply financial intermediaries, while their mutual funds represents mini-banks, if you like, all of which are subject to 100 percent capital requirements.

Explained another way, you hold liquid securities directly and cut out the middleman of the lending bank.Â  It's like expanding the idea of a checkable money market mutual fund to cover the retail banking sector.Â  Here is his short Op-Ed on the idea, here is a Business Week article,Â and here are numerous endorsements for the book.Â  See also Bob Litan on "narrow banking."Â  
I used to advocate a version of this idea myself, but I no longer think it is a good reform proposal, for a few reasons:Â  
1. There aren't enough safe, liquid assets to cover theÂ stock of bank deposits.Â  There would be even fewer safe, liquid assets if fiscal conservatives had their way.Â  And we've now learned that the commercial paper market can seize up and shut down and AAA securities aren't always so safe.
2. Holding T-Bills eliminates the need for the bank intermediary and the resulting problems of moral hazard.Â  But remember â€” these ends are achieved only by lendingÂ that money to the government.Â  What's the old saying?: out of the frying pan, into the fireâ€¦
3.Â A lot of what current banks do would be replicated by non-bank commercial lenders and the risk of the banking sector would be transferred somewhere else.Â  Ideally, these non-bank lenders would engage in greater "maturity-matching," but if banks will exploit the moral hazard problem won't these lenders exploit it too?Â  The financial crisis very much changed my mind on this question.Â  Can't such lenders, to policymakers, appear "too big to fail" in the same way that standard banks do?Â  Are General Motors, AIG, and GE Credit really the path to future financial sector safety?Â  Maybe there is room for improvement, by using more commercial lending, but it is murky and I no longer see a clear gain in this regard.
Here, by the way, is a Bert Ely critique.
title: *Jimmy Stewart is dead*

Iâ€™ve been sick, so watched tv more than usual. Watching Journey to the Center of the Earth, I noticed yet again how folks seem to like adventure stories and games to come with guides. People prefer main characters to follow a trail of clues via a map or book written by someone who has passed before, or at least to follow the advice of a wise old person.

Dante of course provides another example, as does Sibyl and Aeneas.Â  AndÂ Robin's conclusion?:

This has a big lesson for those who like to think of their real life as a grand adventure: relative to fiction, real grand adventures tend to have fewer guides, and more randomness in success. If you want life paths that quickly and reliably reveal your skills, like leveling up in video games, you want artificial worlds like schools, sporting leagues, and corporate fast tracks. Â You might call such lives adventures, but really they pretty much the opposite. Â If you insist instead on adventuring for real, achieving things of real and large consequence against great real obstacles, well then learn to see the glorious nobility of those who try well yet fail.Â

Far from embracing this social democratic model, American Keynesians have criticized it for relying too heavily on exports and not enough on spending and debt. Yet it is not just the decline in the euroâ€˜s value that supports the German resurgence. 
Most of the other euro-zone economies are not having comparable success because they did not make the appropriate investments and reforms. Moreover, the euro is still stronger than its average value since 2001, which suggests that the recent German success is not attributable only to a falling currency. 
In any case, the Germans are exporting much quality machinery and engineering (not just glitzy autos), which can help other nations recover. It is an odd state of affairs when the relatively productive nations are asked to change successful policies because of an economic downturn. 

I would add a few points:
1. I am notÂ sure why the American left so near-unanimously lines up behind Keynesian recommendations these days.Â  (Jeff Sachs is an exception in this regard.)Â  There are other social democratic models for running a government, including that of Germany, and yet a kind of American "can do" spirit pervades our approach to fiscal policy, for better or worse.Â  Commentators make various criticisms of Paul Krugman, but putting the normative aside I find it striking what an American thinker he is, including in his book The Conscience of a Liberal.Â  Someone should write a nice (and non-normative) essay on this point, putting Krugman in proper historical context.

You sometimes hear it said: "Not every nation can run a surplus," or "Can every nation export its way to recovery?"Â  Reword the latter question as "Can every indiviidual trade his way to a higher level of income?" and try answering it again.Â  Productivity-driven exporting really does matter, whether for the individual or the nation.Â  It stabilizes the entire global economy,

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Matt Yglesias suggests the notion is implausible, but I am surprised to read those words.Â  Keep in mind, we have had a recoveryÂ in output, but not in employment.Â  That means a smaller number of laborers are working, but we are producingÂ as much as before.Â  As a simple first cut, how should we measure the marginal product of those now laid-off workers?Â  I would start with the number zero.Â  If a restored level of outputÂ wouldn't count as evidence for the zero marginal product hypothesis, what would?Â  If I ran a business, fired ten people, and output didn't go down, might I start by asking whether those people produced anything useful?
It is true that the ceteris are not paribus,Â  But the observed changes if anything favor the hypothesis of zero marginal product. There has been no major technological breakthrough in the meantime.Â  If anything, there has been bad monetary policy and a dose of regulatory uncertainty.Â  And yet again we can produce just as muchÂ without those workers.Â Â Think of "labor hoarding" yet withoutâ€¦the hoarding.
You might cite oligopoly models and argue that the workers can produce something, but firms won't hire them because they don't want to expand output, due to lack of demand.Â Â That doesn't seem to explain that output hasÂ recovered and that profits are high.Â  And since there is plenty of corporate cash, it isÂ hard to claim that liquidity constraints are preventing the reemployment of those workers.
There is another striking fact about the recession, namely that unemployment isÂ quite low for highly educated workers but about sixteen percentÂ for the less educated workers with no high school degree.Â  (When it comes to income groups, the lowest decile has an unemployment rate of over thirty percent, while it is three percent for the highest decile; I'm not sure of the time horizon for that income measure.)Â  This is consistent with the zero marginal product hypothesis, and yet few analysts ask whether their preferred explanation for unemployment addresses this pattern.
Garett Jones suggests that many unemployed workers are potentially productive, but that businesses do not, at this moment, wantÂ to invest in future productive improvements.Â  The workers only appear to have zero marginal product, because their marginal product lies in future returns not current returns.Â  IÂ see this hypothesis as part of the picture, although I am not sure it explains why current unemployment is so much higherÂ among the unskilled.Â  Is unskilled labor the fundamental capability-builder for the future?Â  I'm not so sure.
It's also interesting to look at the composition of the long-term unemployed (not the same as the composition of all the unemployed, of course).Â Â Older workers with a college education are quite stuck, conditional on their being unemployed.Â  AndÂ in this group,Â more education predicts a longer spell of unemployment.Â  Is this ongoing "recalculation," optimal search theory, or is the roulette wheel simply coming up zero each time it is spun for these workers?Â  Maybe a bit of each.Â  If you want, call some of it age discrimination and relabel the idea "perceived zero marginal product."
In general, which hypotheses predict lots more short-termÂ unemployment among the less educated, but among the long-term unemployed, a disproportionately high degreeÂ of older, more educated people?Â Â This stylized fact seems to point toward search and recalculation ideas, with some zero marginal products tossed in.Â  Do aggregate demand theories yield that same data-matching prediction?Â  I don't see it, at least not without being paired with a theory of concomitant real shocks.
Nothing in the zero marginal product hypothesis requires that these marginal products be zero forever.Â  As the entire economy expands more rapidly (when will that happen?), the value of even a low qualityÂ worker can quicklyÂ become much higher.Â  If you are opening up a new building, suddenly you really need that extra janitor and he is indeed more productive at the new margin.
SomeÂ peopleÂ identify the zero marginal product hypothesis with the "hopeless dregs of the earth" description, but the two are not necessarily the same.Â  Complementarity, combined with some fixed initial factors, can yield zero or near-zero marginal products of labor.Â  (You'llÂ see the phrase "excess capacity" used in this context, though that matches the oligopoly hypothesis more closely.)Â  The "dregs of the earth" view isÂ pessimistic, but the complementarity version of the zero marginal product idea can be quite optimistic, predicting a very rapid recovery in the labor market, once the interactionsÂ turn positive.Â  
The "dregs" and the "complementarities" views alsoÂ haveÂ different policy recommendations.Â  The dregs view implies either hopelessness or a lot of fundamental retraining or ongoing assistance, while the complementarity view leads one to ask how we might mobilize positive complementarities (rather than leaving orphaned factors of production)Â more quickly.Â  PerhapsÂ there are some fixed factors, such as managerial oversight, and entrepreneurs do not wantÂ to strain those fixed factors too hard.Â  How can we make such fixed factors more replicable or more flexible?
Addendum: Arnold Kling comments.
title: Zero marginal product workers

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
I found this short essay worth a read.Â  Excerpt:

The lack of capital generation is therefore the most serious implication of Greek geography. Situated as far from global flows of capital as any European country that considers itself part of the West, Greece finds itself surrounded by sheltered ports, most of which are protected by mountains and cliffs that drop off into the sea. This affords Greece little room for population growth, and contributes to its inability to produce much domestic capital. This, combined with the regionalized approach to political authority encouraged by mountainous geography, has made Greece a country that has been inefficiently distributing what little capital it has had for millennia.
Countries that have low capital growth and considerable infrastructural costs usually tend to develop a very uneven distribution of wealth. The reason is simple: Those who have access to capital get to build and control vital infrastructure and thereby make the decisions both in public and working life. In countries that have to import capital, this becomes even more pronounced, since those who control industries and businesses that bring in foreign cash have more control than those who control fixed infrastructure, which can always be nationalized (industries and businesses can move elsewhere if threatened with nationalization). When such uneven distribution of wealth is entrenched in a society, a serious labor-capital (or, in the European context, a left-right) split emerges. This is why Greece is politically similar to Latin American countries, which face the same infrastructural and capital problems, right down to periods of military rule and an ongoing and vicious labor-capital split.
Despite the limitations on its capital generation, Greece has no alternative but to create an expensive defensive capability that allows it to control the Aegean Sea. Put simply, the core of Greece is neither the breadbaskets of Thessaly and Greek Macedonia, nor the Athens-Piraeus metropolitan area, where around half of the population lives. The core of Greece is the Aegean Sea â€“ the actual water, not the coastland â€“ which allows these three critical areas of Greece to be connected for trade, defense and communication. Control of the Aegean also gives Greece the additional benefit of influencing trade between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Without control of the Aegean, there simply is no Greece.

The essay is interesting throughout.Â  I thank a loyal MR reader for the pointer, sadly I misplaced your name in the move back from Germany.
title: The geopolitics of Greece

I have never heard aÂ market-oriented economist argue that aÂ riseÂ in the minimum wage boosts the demand for labor.Â  You might try this argument: "The government is certifying that these workers are worth this much.Â  The government is defining the market price.Â  Entrepreneurs will believe that price and hire workers in the expectation of finding an equivalent or even superior marginal product.Â  The government said that was the right price."Â  
No go.Â Â Market-oriented economistsÂ instead claimÂ that entrepreneurs "see through" to the real marginal products of these laborers.Â  The demand for labor, rather than rising, would fall and unemployment would result.
So what happens when the Fed "sets" short-term interest rates or influences other prices?Â  What is postulated by monetary misperceptions theories, including Austrian business cycle theory?Â  Entrepreneurs no longer see through to the fundamentals.Â  Instead, entrepreneursÂ are taken to believe this Fed-influenced rate is the correct price and they makeÂ their plans accordingly.
What is the difference between these two cases?Â  I believe we need a better theory of when people take price signals as informative and when not.Â  Too often people just assume that the inferential abilities, or lack thereof, goÂ the way they wantÂ them to.

In fact, we have some pretty good historical dataÂ on this issue. Bearing in mind that observatories are an early form of space exploration, Alex MacDonald, a NASA research economist, notes:
For the majority of its history, space exploration in America has been funded privately. The trend

â€¦rather than scaling the expenditure as a share of the total resources of the U.S. economy, the expenditure can be scaled as a share of the resources of the individuals who undertook the projects. author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Here's an NYT forum on the issue.Â  Here is a recent Megan McArdle blog post.Â  Traditionally I've been sympathetic to tenure (disclaimer: I have it), in part because the schools which have done away with it â€” the for-profits â€” have carved out a big niche but they have not displaced traditional non-profit, tenure-driven higher education in most fields.Â  Few parents dream of sending their kids there.Â  My point today is simply to note that tenure critics have yet to spell out what the alternative â€” and thus the debate â€” really looks like.
If youÂ argue "abolish tenure"Â the real question is this: under what conditions will professors be fired?Â  For instance, if you abolish tenure but never fire a professor, the change is maybe not so large (though the threat to fire still can change equilibria).
Here's a thought experiment: takeÂ a 53-year-old professor, at a moderate qualityÂ university, who goes from publishing three articles a year to one article a year, and in somewhat lesser journals than before.Â  His teaching evaluations slip steadily, though he never becomes a disaster in the classroom.Â  In the no-tenure world, does that person get fired?Â  (And what's his chance of finding another job?)
If firing is in order, how much higher do initial wage offers have to be?Â  (Recall that you're asking the new hire to take a $$ wage lower than his human capital would otherwise indicate; btw Megan covers that query here.)Â  Is this deal worth it for universities?Â  If that guy doesn't get laid off, who does?Â Â Only the convicted felons?
If you believe in abolishing tenure, and yet tenure won't go away, do you also think schools should cut entry-level wages for new professors, as a second-best means of loweringÂ their total compensation?Â  How do you feel about the achievement paths of the schools that are already trying this strategy?Â  Will abolishing tenure involve any compensation scheme other than that already used by current for-profits in higher education?
With the pro-tenureÂ arguments, you might wonder how higher education is supposed to differ fromÂ other sectors of the economy.Â  I believe it is this:Â given that higher education is in part about signaling and certification, socialization and networking of students, "warm glow" of the donors, and research superstars, the later-period shirking of the typical laggard doesn't hurt actual productivity nearly as much as the schools themselves might like toÂ think.Â  
This also suggests that schools themselves will never make an intellectually convincing case for tenure, since they can't come out and admit that "in the longer run, most of us don't really matter, we only pretended our productivity was worth something in the first place."Â  Education as theatre, and all that; see my The Age of the Infovore.
When I hear answers to the aboveÂ questions, namely what the alternative to tenure looks like, then the tenure debate will be getting somewhere.
To some extent the proposed gains from abolishing tenure can be reaped simply by increasing teaching load, relying more on on-line instruction and/or reintroducing mandatory retirement.
title: What if universities get rid of tenure?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Krugman (here), Rogoff, DeLong, and others all have recent writings on this topic.Â Â My general view on these matters is the following:
1. There is nothing sacred about "90 percent" as a cut-off ratio and in any case such structural quantitative estimates are not stable over time.Â  The accompanying expectations matter too.
2. The United States today (and in many other times) can manage a ratio higher than that; how much higher we do not know and what is the correct "stopping rule" we do not know.Â  I suppose we will find out.
3. Major wars aside, if the United States approached or exceeded the 90 percent figure, it would be a sign of a dysfunctional politics and an irresponsible citizenry.Â  Do we have to borrow that much money?Â  Can't we just pay for the stuff?Â  Apparently not.
4. Even if the debt is not itself a problem, being skeptical aboutÂ the debt is one way to enforce accountability on the expenditure side, namely by requiring transparency on expenditures and who is really footing the bill for what.
5. If the United States reaches or exceeds that ninety percent ratio, which is likely, it will be because of health care costs, spending too much on health care, and having dysfunctional health care institutions.
6. Under the scenario of #5, measured gdp might do OK.Â  Health care costs are part of gdp too.Â  But we will be misallocating resources on a massive scale and the high debt helped makeÂ it possible.
7. At some sufficiently high debt-gdp ratio, it becomes a foreign policy issue and a big one.Â  Postwar UK had a high debt to gdp ratio, and to this day it is a fine place, but that debt meant the end of England as a world power, for better or worse.Â  The U.S. for instance used financial issuesÂ to push England around and they basically had to give up on their overseas commitments.Â  A very high debt ratio here would mean the end of the U.S. as a global world power, again even if gdp does OK.Â Â A global power needs the option of spending a lot more, quickly, without asking for anyone's permission.Â  Your mileage on a U.S. retreat from the global policeman role will vary, but it's the elephant in the room which hardly anyone is talking about.
8. I don't agree with Jim Buchanan on either a balanced budget amendment (I am against it, preferring deficits in recessions), or on the intergenerational incidence of domestic debt.Â  Nonetheless his writings are an undervalued resource in this debate.Â  Very often he focuses on what debt does to a country, drawing upon the Founding Fathers, the classical economists, and the Italian public finance theorists, among others.
Addendum: Ezra Klein comments.
title: Whatâ€™s the critical debt-gdp ratio?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Andrew West, citing Charlie Stross, sends along a question:

What is the minimum number of people you need in order to maintain (not necessarily to extend) our current level of technological civilization?

I'll treat this as a steady-state question and not commit to any particular time frame.Â Â Stross wrote:

I'd put an upper bound of about one billion on the range, because that encompasses basically the entire population of NAFTA and the EU, with Japan, Taiwan, and the industrial enterprise zones of China thrown in for good measure. (While China is significant, more than half of its population is still agrarian, hence not providing inputs to this system).
I'd put a lower bound of 100 million on the range, too. The specialities required for a civil aviation sector alone may well run to half a million people; let's not underestimate the needs of raw material extraction and processing (from crude oil to yttrium and lanthanum), of a higher education/research sector to keep training the people we need in order to replenish small pools of working expertise, and so on. Hypothetically, we may only need 500 people in one particular niche, but that means training 20 of them a year to keep the pool going, plus future trainers, and an allowance for wastage and drop-outs by people who made a bad career choice. 

MyÂ casual, seat-of-the-pantsÂ estimate is that a world of one billion people â€” mostly from the wealthier countries â€” would be about fifteenÂ percent poorer for those people than today's world.Â  Even very poor countries often supply valuable commodities or raw materials, in addition to buying some exports and expanding the scope of both comparataive advantage and increasing returns.Â  What's the implicit assumption about settling those countries and reaping those resources?Â  Are we dealingÂ with a Nigerian government backed by five million very poor Nigerians?Â  Or is Nigeria an empty land, open to settlement as a southern colony of Switzerland?Â  I am assuming the former and that means those countries have much smaller economies, and higher fixed cost problems, than today.
Under this scenario the United States loses much of its Asian immigration and Arab immigration, two successes even if you disagree with me about the successes of Latino immigration.
Alternatively, the thought experiment could be shrinking the world's population but keeping the rich-poor proportion constant in the population.Â  In that case the number ofÂ people needed to maintain current standards of living, or even fifteen percent less,Â is much higher.
title: How many people are needed to maintain current living standards?
