author: Tyler Cowen
text:
For me, pluots and grapes are close substitutes, though not perfect substitutes.
Let's say a house visitor brings a big bag of pluots as a gift.Â  That distorts my optimum pluot-grape ratio.Â  But I don't eat all the pluots at once, simply to restore the preferred ratio.Â  That would be an unbalanced meal.Â  Instead, I dig into the pluot bag at a higher rate than I would normally eat pluots.Â  Over a longer period of time the proper ratio is restored, pluotÂ by pluot.Â  
The closer pluots and grapesÂ are as substitutes, the longer itÂ takes for equilibrium restoration.Â  But the closeness of substitution is not always the major factor determining the speed of adjustment.Â  It may be just as important, or more important, how hungry I am, how much of a glutton I am,Â and how much I like pluots.Â  It also matters whether I am fearing a largeÂ shock, requiring a majorÂ pluot reserve, such as when a bevy of pluot-devouring guests might suddenly visit the house.Â Â 
In any case, equilibrium restoration eventually comes.Â  Those pluots will clear my refrigerator, sooner or later.
Apply a similarÂ analysis to cash and T-Bills.Â  At low nominal interest rates they are close substitutes but not perfect substitutes.Â  T-Bills areÂ of greater use for clearinghouse collateral, and yield a bit more, but they are not liquid in exactly the same ways.Â  Even if cash and T-Bills are close substitutes, monetary policyÂ will change the banks'Â mix and so banks eventually will reequilibrate, converting extra cash into AD, one way or another.Â  But as with the pluot adjustment, this won't happen all at once.
Equilibration (and the accompanying AD boost) may be slow, maybe too slow for comfort.Â  But the degree of substitutability is not the only factor determining the speed of this adjustment, just as with the pluots.Â Â  The degree of bank and business confidence may be the most important factor.Â  Other factors will be the cues from the Fed, the corporate cultures of the banks, possible uncertainty, transactional frictions (the difference in returns is small but perhaps the cost of adjusting is small too), and so on.Â Â The degree of substitutability is one factor determining the speed of adjustment but not necessarily a major factor.Â  I am not sure it should be putÂ in the top three most important factors.
The zero bound argument assumes that the degree of substitutability is, at current margins, the major factor which matters.Â Â You are being "sold" a model of portfolio adjustment with one dominant factor.
Monetary policy is not working well today, but perhaps bank and business confidence is aÂ bigger reason than the degree of substitutability.Â  From those who promote the relevance of the "zero bound" argument, you will see it implicitly assumed that we have a case of perfect substitutes and thatÂ substitutability is the major factor hindering portfolio adjustment, as would lead to anÂ expansion of the broader money supply aggregates.
In many models "close substitutes" and "perfect substitutes" haveÂ very differentÂ properties.Â  Current discussions of the liquidity trap usually neglect this point.
Addendum: This is also a framework for thinking aboutÂ ceasing to pay interest on reserves.Â  If it creates perfect substitutes, stop the policy immediately.Â  If it creates closer substitutes, it may matter much less.
title: Close substitutes vs. perfect substitutes

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
There are two measures of fiscal policy: the sum total of everything a government does and the "ramp-up-the-spending-quickly" component which gets labeled "stimulus" by politicians and the media.
In the blogosphere, economists argue mostly about the latter yet it is the former which isÂ more important.Â  (On this question, among others,Â I credit Yglesias for being ahead of most of the economists.)
The most important, most effective, and least controversial forms of fiscal policy are the automatic stabilizers.Â  Let's say you have two countries, A and B.Â  In country A government spends 50 percent of gdp, mostly on a well-designed welfare state.Â  When the downturn comes, there is only enough extra borrowing to make up for the lost revenue, and there is no designed "stimulus" per se.Â  In country B, government spends 25 percent of gdp, mostly not on a well-designed welfare state.Â  When the downturn comes, country B does an extra three, four, or evenÂ five percent of gdp "ramp-up" borrowing and spending.
Which country has a better, more active, and more AD-stabilizing fiscal policy?Â  Well, it depends on the details and the numbers but I would encourage you to considerÂ country A for this honor.
I don't agree with Krugman's recent interpretation that "Korea and China both engaged in much more aggressive stimulus than any Western nation â€“ and it has worked out well."
In South Korea the welfare state is smallerÂ and moreÂ of the government spendingÂ is corporate and military, compared to Western Europe, plus government spending is lower overall.Â  In China central government spending is 19.9Â percent of gdp (beware those numbers, though) and the social welfare state institutions, and automatic stabilizers, are very weak, both in terms of quantity and quality.Â  
For purposes of contrast, in Germany government spending is about 44 percent of gdpÂ and you'll find similar or higher number across Western Europe.
I think of Korea and China as having more "ramp-up" stimulus to make up for what is initially a weaker fiscal policy all things considered (you can add Russia to that list, which also has a high measured "ramp-up" stimulus).Â  Overall, despite the bigger "make-up."Â it is quite possibleÂ Korea and ChinaÂ are doing less with fiscal policy to stabilize aggregate demand than are the more substantive welfare states.Â  (Also see Sumner's comment on Krugman here.)
Or think about the fiscal variation within Europe.Â  "Ramp-up" spending measures of zero vs. 1.5 percent of gdp are portrayed as big differences, but as a chunk of the broader metric â€” the variation in AD-stabilizing properties of the public sectorÂ â€“ it's not such a big deal, especially once you takeÂ "crowding out" into account.Â  Whichever quantity of ramp-up spending you prefer, it's not reason to preach doom and gloom for the welfare stateÂ countries with the smallerÂ ramp-up plans.Â  (Have I mentioned that ramp-up spending is often of lower quality?)
The best fiscal policy â€” for cyclical and not justÂ growth reasons â€” is a steady stream of permanent and high-quality government expenditures.Â  That's true no matter what you think the absolute size of this flow should be.
Sometimes you will see this point acknowledged, such as when U.S. federal transfers to the states are praised as the most effective part of ARRA (which they were).Â  But again, that's just a constant stream of spending.Â  And that's in the particulars, not just the aggregate, and it matters because you don't want the federal spending having to rehire the people the states laid off.Â  The praiseÂ is correct, but rarely are its complete implications thought through and presented.
Let's say we measure the efficacy of fiscal policy correctly.Â  The countries with the most stabilizingÂ fiscal policiesÂ would be the big government welfare states with high quality governments.Â  That means Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Netherlands, and so on, the usual list.Â  In addition to theirÂ relatively high quality governments, they also have relatively strong real economies and healthy institutions.
When this whole episode is over, I would not be surprised to see that same list of countries as having had relatively good recoveries (of course we don't know yet).Â  A regression could positively correlate "good final outcomes from the crisis" with "total fiscal policy, properly measured."Â  Such a regression also would be picking up the quality of the institutions and of the real economy.
One way of reading those (potential) numbersÂ would argue that strong real economies, strong governments, and healthy institutions all go togetherÂ and that such combinations help drive healthy recoveries.Â  That's actually not so far from real business cycle theory, a favorite whipping boy but in its more sophisticated forms alive and well.Â Â 
In the blogosphere, most of what you hear about "fiscal policy" â€” pro or con â€” isÂ misconceiving and mismeasuring the concept and then drawing incorrect conclusions.Â  There's no good reason to focus our economic attention, or perform the informal (or formal) econometrics,Â on the "ramp-up spending" component.Â  The ramp-up spendingÂ attracts a lot of symbolic interest in the more partisan political debates because it has Obama's or Merkel's or whosever name on it, but it is better to see through suchÂ labeling.
Keep your eyes on the ball(s): high quality governments, stabilizing long-run expenditures, well-designed welfare states,Â robust real economies, and healthyÂ institutions.Â  In principle there's plenty of room for those concepts in Keynesian economics, but right now they're gettingâ€¦crowded outâ€¦in the intellectual debate.
title: Measuring fiscal policy and evaluating its results

author: Alex Tabarrok

InÂ Preachers who are not believers,Â a provocative new paper in Evolutionary Psychology,Â Daniel Dennett and Linda LaScola interview five preachers who no longer believe in God. Â Here's one bit:

A gulf opened up between what one says from the pulpit and what one has been taught in seminary. This gulf is well-known in religious circles. The eminent biblical scholar Bart D. Ehrmanâ€™s widely read book, Misquoting Jesus (2005), recounts his own odyssey from the seminary into secular scholarship, beginning in the Moody Bible Institute in Chicago, a famously conservative seminary which required its professors to sign a statement declaring the Bible to be the inerrant word of God, a declaration that was increasingly hard for Ehrman to underwrite by his own research. The Dishonest Church (2003), by retired United Church of Christ minister, Jack Good, explores this â€œtragic divideâ€� that poisons the relationship between the laity and the clergy. Every Christian minister, not just those in our little study, has to confront this awkwardness, and no doubt there are many more ways of responding to it than our small sample illustrates. How widespread is this phenomenon? When we asked one of the other pastors we talked with initially if he thought clergy with his views were rare in the church, he responded, â€œOh, you canâ€™t go through seminary and come out believing in God!â€� Surely an overstatement, but a telling one. As Wes put it:


â€¦there are a lot of clergy out there who â€” if you were to ask them â€” if you were to list the five things that you think may be the most central beliefs of Christianity, they would reject every one of them.


One can be initiated into a conspiracy without a single word exchanged or secret handshake; all it takes is the dawning realization, beginning in seminary, that you and the others are privy to a secret, and that they know that you know, and you know that they know that you know. This is what is known to philosophers and linguists as mutual knowledge, and it plays a potent role in many social circumstances. Without any explicit agreement, mutual knowledge seals the deal: you then have no right to betray this bond by unilaterally divulging it, or even discussing it.

It was interesting to me that this account is related to the ideas of preference falsificationÂ developed by Timur Kuran, sacrifice and stigmaÂ developed by Larry IannacconeÂ and common knowledgeÂ by Robert Aumann.

If only mentally, I predicted a worse summer for the European economies than they seem to beÂ experiencing; furthermore the euro is back up in the 1.30 range.Â  Why was I wrong?Â  I was believing those economies have more wage stickiness than they actually do.Â  In this regard a lot of Keynesians and market-oriented economists have been making similar mistakes, albeit forÂ different reasons.Â  Sticky wages are a core part of the KeynesianÂ worldview, whereas many non-KeynesianÂ economists are quite skeptical of European labor markets and their inflexibilities.
These days I browse British, Irish, Spanish and German newspapers with reasonable frequency.Â  I am struck by how many accounts of falling nominal and real wages I see.Â Â Outside of Germany, the proverbial cat hasn't quite bounced, but it seems to haveÂ hit the pavement.
One theory is that most wages are actually fairlyÂ flexible, but we don't usually like to cutÂ wages or have wagesÂ fall.Â  When needed, many wagesÂ can fall quite readily.Â  In other words, sometimes it is easier to cut wages by a lot than by a little.
I hardly think the European economies, or the Euro, are in the clear.Â  Differential rates of productivity growth, and the absence and impossibility of a common fiscal sovereign, still will make the arrangement unworkable.Â  But it's worth explicitly noting that so far my forecast has been off the track.

author: Alex Tabarrok
text:
A number of people (Slacktivist, Kevin Drum, Matt Yglesias, Megan Mcardle) are debating the use of credit scores in employment. Â Credit scores are useful at predicting all kinds of things including, for example, car accidents so there is good reason to believe that they are useful in employment. The above commentators tend to focus on the potential for scores to hurt the poor but that is not obvious.Â  Consider a similar issue: Should employers be allowed to use background criminal checks when hiring?
One argument against is that black men are more likely to have criminal backgrounds and thus these criminal background checks discriminate against black men.Â  Let's put aside the normative issues. Whatâ€™s surprising is that under plausible circumstances criminal background checks can lead to an increase in the employment of black men. The reason is that without the background check employers face a risk that their employees are ex-cons. If employers are very averse to hiring ex-cons then they will seek to reduce this risk and one way of doing so is by not hiring any black men. As a result, a background check allows non ex-cons to distinguish themselves from the pack and to be hired. Furthermore, when background checks exist, non ex-cons know that they will not face statistical discrimination and thus have an increased incentive to invest in skills.
Consistent with this reasoning, although not demonstrative of the net effect,Â Holzer, Raphael and Stoll find that:

â€¦employers who check criminal backgrounds are more likely to hire
African American workers, especially men. This effect is stronger among
those employers who report an aversion to hiring those with criminal
records than among those who do not.


My view is actually that criminals face too many post-crime impediments to reintegrating themselves within the workforce.Â  Private incentives not to take a risk on an ex-con do not cohere with social incentives to reintegrate workers into society and thus we get too little hiring of ex-cons.Â  As a result, ex-cons face a low opportunity cost of recidivism.
Nevertheless, banning criminal background checks or credit scores is probably not the best way to combat these types of problem.Â  Banning criminal background checks increases the incentive to rely on less accurate statistical discrimination which discriminates against the innocent and reduces the incentive to invest in skills.Â  In short, hiding the bad apples among the good comes at the expense of the good.
title: Credit Scores, Criminal Background Checks and Hiding the Bad Apples

I read someone, somewhereÂ arguing that Elizabeth Warren was the nominee to shut them down.Â  I am curious about the modern liberal take on autonomy and credit.Â  Let's say that two gay men, of unknown health status,Â want to have informed, consensual, unprotected sex.Â  Should the law prohibit this?Â  I believe the answer is no.Â  Furthermore it is not just a matter of enforcement difficulty, it is a question of autonomy.Â  If you don't think so, modifyÂ the example so that two heterosexualÂ people want to have consensual but unprotected sex.Â  And so on.
The unprotected sex is riskier and less prudent than borrowing money at an annualized rate of two hundred percent.Â  Why prohibit one and not the other?Â Â Many of the borrowers are being fooled, but others have legitimate reasons to seek the money, such as wanting to buy a birthday present for a visit to one's child, living with a separated spouse.
Is it that sex is sacred but borrowing money is not?Â  What if you're borrowing money to catch a plane to go have sex?Â  Isn't sex a big reason why people might borrow money at high annualized rates?Â  Aren't "sex decisions" some of the least rational we make and the most prone to error?
When I use the ATM, often I am outside the network and thus I am paying annualized interest rates of over two hundred percent a year.Â  Should someone (other than Natasha) stop me?Â  Should they only stop me when I am younger and poorer than is the current Tyler?Â  What about equality before the law?
How many of you would support this same woman â€” with enthusiasm â€” if she wanted to banÂ risky but consensual sex?

I prefer to call it a carbon tax, while admitting the two are sometimes equivalent.Â  Here is Ross's key passage:

Spending 1 percent of our G.D.P. as a hedge against catastrophe might make sense; spending the same amount without any prospect of actually getting that insurance policy seems like idealistic folly. And so far, when it comes to actual mechanisms whereby Waxman-Markey becomes a model for the developing world, all Iâ€™ve heard from the left are neoconservative-style arguments about how â€œif the worldâ€™s leading power leads, everyone else will follow,â€� and visions of a carbon trade war between the West and China. Neither seems persuasive.

That's a strong argument, but the case for a carbon tax remains threefold:
1. Even if we cut government spending a lot, some taxes will have to go up.Â  This seems like the least bad tax to raise or create, since it has some chance of producing a better outcome.Â  It's hard to say that about most of the other potential tax boosts.Â  I'd also cut the tax deduction for mortgage interest, of course.Â  That too could improve the quality of outcomes.
2. Given that American policies are contributing to a (probabilistic) climate-basedÂ "attack" on Bangladesh and numerous other countries, there is a deontological case for trying to stop that attack.Â  It is a libertarian rights violation issue, driven by all of us in our role as consumers.Â Â Â  
It is a practical response â€” but to me a morally weak one â€” to argue "We AmericansÂ are the wealthiest country in the world but we're not competent enough to stop our contribution to the problem, so we're not going to try."Â  I get the logic, and I even agree with the predictive pessimism, but I'm not comfortable staying put with that as my final position.
3. A carbon tax might lead to a new green technology, with high upfront costs and low marginal costs.Â  Some of the rest of the world might then adopt the technology, even if those countries don't ever adopt a carbon tax.Â  In the short run this seems a little pie-in-the-sky, but in the longer run is it so crazy?Â  Haven't the Chinese adopted most of our other technological innovations?
That all said, I still don't like Waxman-Markey and in that regard I agree with Ross.Â  The billÂ seems to bureaucratize the energy sector, forgo most of the revenue opportunities, produce massive time consistency problems (postpone real adjustment and then give out more permits over time), and allÂ without getting public buy-in to the idea of higher carbonÂ prices.Â  
I'll also stress â€” again â€” that a carbon tax needs to be combined with the strong deregulation of the energy sector, and the weakening of NIMBY, in particular for wind power.
p.s. I hear less often these days aboutÂ the "global cooling trend."

text:
The link is here, here is the abstract:

Gypsies believe the lower half of the human body is invisibly polluted, that supernatural defilement is physically contagious, and that non-Gypsies are spiritually toxic. I argue that Gypsies use these beliefs, which on the surface regulate their invisible world, to regulate their visible one. They use superstition to create and enforce law and order. Gypsies do this in three ways. First, they make worldly crimes supernatural ones, leveraging fear of the latter to prevent the former. Second, they marshal the belief that spiritual pollution is contagious to incentivize collective punishment of antisocial behavior. Third, they recruit the belief that non-Gypsies are supernatural cesspools to augment such punishment. Gypsies use superstition to substitute for traditional institutions of law and order. Their bizarre belief system is an efficient institutional response to the constraints they face on their choice of mechanisms of social control. 

Steve Levitt bloggedÂ the paperÂ here.Â  Relative to Peter, I am much more likely to find social institutions inefficient.Â  I think individual decisions are often inefficient for behavioral reasons and furthermore individual norms often produce bad or dysfunctional outcomes when multiplied at the social level.Â  Historically, most of human history has been lived under conditions of extreme poverty and misery, aÂ warning sign of potential inefficiency.
I don't have any personal opinion about gypsies (about whom I know little), but just from reading Peter's paper (or abstract) I thought he should have called it "Why gypsies are inefficient."Â  I received the impression that a more efficient set of gypsy norms would do more to encourage integration and education, especially when gypsies live in wealthier, freer countries.Â  I don't doubt that some of the norms are partially functional, relative to the poverty, but some of the norms also seem to support the poverty.

author: Alex Tabarrok

Theories of unemployed labor are a subset of theories of unemployed resources.Â  
The U.S. housing vacancy rateâ€“an unemployment rate for homesâ€“is at its highest level since at least 1965 (see figure).Â  Why?Â  Is it sticky prices? Lack of aggregate demand? Structural?

  House prices may be sticky but they have fallen a lotâ€“maybe not enoughâ€“but they have fallen a lot more than have wages.Â  On the other hand, house prices rose a lot more than wages. Maybe house prices are sticky relative to the required variation in market clearing levels.
What about lack of aggregate demand?Â  The homeownership rate was 67.2 in 2000 and today itâ€™s 66.9.Â  Thus, we donâ€™t have too great a supply of houses in the aggregate so aggregate demand is likely a factor.
Is the problem structural?Â  It does seem that we have too many houses in the South and the West where the boom was concentrated.Â  If we think of the unemployment rate as a measure of where there are too many houses then the following figure shows that there is a positive correlation between the home vacancy rate and the unemployment rate.Â  Itâ€™s not as tight as one might expect, however.Â  California, for example, has a high unemployment rate but a home vacancy rate slightly below the national average and many states such as Wisconsin have plenty of unemployment but a very low home vacancy rate.

Â 
My guesstimate is 50% AD, 25% sticky prices, 25% structural. Â Tyler would read it differently. I do think more progress could be made if greater attention were given to theories of unemployed resources and not just unemployed labor.
title: Why are so many homes unemployed?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
I'd like to get a few opinions on record or simply recap some previousÂ points.
The current downturn is a mix of AD and real shocks, inÂ uncertain proportions, and in a manner which is hard to separate empirically.Â  It is now obvious there is a lot of structural unemployment and there is a quick and probably unjustified rush to define it all as AD-influenced unemployment turned sour.Â  The structural theories have their problems, but they can betterÂ explain why corporate profits are highÂ and can better explain the distribution of unemployment across income and educational classes.Â  The regional distribution of unemployment isÂ persisting because of labor immobility, which involves bothÂ AD and structural issues.Â  The sectoral shift view is more about shifting out of optimism-linked activities, within any particular sector,Â rather than about shifting out of construction and financeÂ per se.
The mix of structural and AD factors does not, in any case, support liquidationist policies.Â  It supports AD-stabilizing policies, though it suggests that in absolute terms those policies will do less well than expected.Â  The failure of the fiscal stimulus is consistent with a number of different views, not just the claim that it should have been bigger.Â  We've yet to see a good theory of how stimulus scales up to produce a bigger and better multiplier at higher levels.
I don't trust stimulus analysesÂ which fail to assign a central role to confidence andÂ confidence is hard to model.
Current experience is also consistent with (but not unambiguously favoring) an Austrian-like view that the stimulus boosts some activity and then shortly thereafter pulls away the rug, leaving us more or less back where we started, albeit with some smoothing gains in the short run and some adjustment costs in the longer run.Â  The persistence andÂ scale-up from the initial fiscal boost is hardly guaranteed.Â  The empirical papers on multipliers are not to be trusted and the results are in any case hard to generalize from one period to another.
Harald Uhlig's paper is oneÂ statement of the case against stimulus.Â  There is nothing measured by the Alan Blinder study which rules out the central result of this paper, namely transitory gains in the short run and high costs in the longer run.
Macroeconomics is rarely simple.Â Â 
Elizabeth Warren is unlikely to prove an effective agency head, and the two sides to this debate ought to switch positions.Â  Yetâ€¦politics very often isn't about policy.
On the AD front, Scott SumnerÂ has been vindicated more than any other writer.Â Â His best critic is Arnold Kling, especially with regard to whether there are only two kinds of inflation regimes, low or high and variable.Â Â A related question is what a looser monetary policy would have done to financing the long-run debt burden and the use ofÂ the interest rate spread to recapitalize banks.Â Â 
We still don't know what we are doing.

Andrew Wylie has decided to become a publisherâ€¦I am appalled, however, that Andrew has chosen to give his list exclusively to a single retailer.

That is from the president of Macmillan, Wylie is a famous agent, the topic is eBooks, and the retailerÂ of course is Amazon.Â  The authors in this newly consummated deal include John Updike and Philip Roth.
GivingÂ Amazon exclusive rights boosts theirÂ incentive to market the book.Â  For books there is significant "spillover" demand through consumer word-of-mouth, but in this case all the recommendations will lead to purchases at Amazon and none to Barnes and Noble.Â  On the downside, you lose sales to people who don't buy through Amazon, but for eBooks how many people can that be these days?Â  You also lose spillover sales fromÂ the marketing of other, now-excluded retailers, such as Sony eBooks.Â  Maybe that's small potatoes.
If the president of Macmillan is upset,Â he fears the AmazonÂ marketing will drain demand from his titles.Â  (Bookstores are upset too.)Â  If I were Wylie, his letter would have me cackling with glee.Â  
For a while.Â  Does WylieÂ knowÂ he is the next middleman to be cut out of the deal?Â  His agent-like services are more valuableÂ to the extent there are competing bidders for the book rights.Â  The only question is whether the authors (or their estates) will squeeze him or Amazon will squeeze him, or both.
(You might think that Wylie would gain by extending the market power of the authors to market power at the retail level.Â  The economic theory of "double marginalization" shows this won't work and that the market power of Amazon cannotÂ benefitÂ the upstream rights holder, who does best by seeking out competitive retail and charging a higher transfer price for the IP rights.)
Antitrust aside,Â does competition constrain Amazon from acquiring ever more eBook titles in this fashion?Â Â It works for Amazon only if their (potentially) stronger marketing increases net sales and thus increases output.Â  It's easy enough for that marketing to work for any single set of titles, especially when accompanied by all this publicity.Â  It's much harder for that marketing push to work for books as a whole and therefore there is a natural check on how much of the market Amazon will lock upÂ in this fashion.
Got eBook, anyone?
IÂ thank S. for the pointer.

The author is C. Bradley Thompson and this new book is in broad termsÂ an Objectivist ("Randian") critique of neoconservatism and Leo Strauss.Â  Here is one summary bit:

Inevitably, the neocons are epistemological relativists (though of an anti-egalitarian nature), which is the source, as we shall see momentarily, of their moral relativism.Â  Because the political good in their world is mutable and always changing, the neoconservatives do not want fixed principles to which they are hbeholden, nor do they strive to be morally or politically consistent.Â  Their power and authority is generated and sustained by the illusion that the world is in a state of constant change and that it is governed by what Machiavelli called fortuna.Â  The truth or falsity of an idea is, according to the neocons, determined by its usefulness in a particular situation and for particular people.Â  What is true today, they argue, may not be true tomorrow if an idea or an action fails to work in new and different situations.Â  In such a world, there can be no certainty, no absolutes, no fixed moral principles.

The authorÂ writes â€” correctly â€“Â "hoi polloi," instead of theÂ redundant "the hoi polloi."
Thompson argues that Leo Strauss showed sympathies for the Italian fascism of Mussolini, at least relative to liberalism and religion.
At timesÂ the bookÂ sounds like Bryan Caplan criticizing me, though I takeÂ such ripostesÂ to say more about Bryan than about me.
When I was young, I very much enjoyed reading John Robbins's Calvinist answer to Ayn RandÂ (revised here), even though I did not agree with much of it.Â  I often learn more when ideas clash in relatively stark forms.
In my view, principles and politics don't always mix but the problem is neither epistemological nor moral.Â  Ill-informed voters, especially in diverse societies, can only swallow so much in the form of principle.Â  If one is committed to intellectual discourse, butÂ within the range of the politically feasible, a lot of intellectual principle is difficult to sustain.Â  I do believe in principles, but I don't see that any point of view has overcome this quite general problem.Â  In that sense I do not blameÂ neoconservatism per se.Â  But am I a neoconservative?Â  No, and Brad's book gives some of the reasons why not.

The author is Sonia Shah and the subtitle is How Malaria has Ruled Humankind for 500,000 Years.Â  Excerpt:

The mosquito's immune system instinctively attacks the parasite, encapsulating the intruder in scabs and bombarding it with toxic chemicals.Â  To survive, the parasite must unleash armies of progeny in such massive numbers that fighting it off becomes more trouble than it's worth.Â  Male and female forms of the parasite, called gametocytes, then fuse, and the resulting parasites create cysts that cling to the walls of the bug's gut.Â  (The spasmodic waving of the male gametocyte's long tail, which precedes the act of fusing with the female â€” yes, this microbe reproduces sexually as well as asexually â€” is called exflagellation.)Â  Tens of thousands of slithering threads explode from the cysts and swarm up to the mosquito's salivary gland.Â  This is the form of parasite must take to infect human beings.Â  Malariologists call it the sporozoite.Â  When a mosquito starts a blood feed, some two dozen slivery sporozoites will escape into their next host.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Most firms try to sell their initial public offerings at predetermined prices, rather than just holding an auction.Â  After the shares are sold, there appear to be immediate excess returns, which suggests some money may have been left on the table.Â  Why do things this way?
Ravi Jagannathan, Andrei Jirnyi, and Ann Sherman have a new and comprehensive study (NBER) of this long-standing question.Â  Here is the abstract:

At least 25 countries have used IPO auctions, but most have since abandoned them. We argue that this is because auctions, being indirect mechanisms, require a level of sophistication above that of many investors. Through suitably calibrated examples, we show that even sophisticated investors can make mistakes while bidding in auctions, especially when facing uncertainty about the number and type of bidders, and such mistakes impose costs on other participants. We provide empirical support for our arguments. IPO auctions have been plagued by unexpectedly large fluctuations in the number of participants, return chasing investors, and high-bidding free riders. Our analysis suggests that a direct mechanism that resembles a transparent version of book building would be preferable to auctions.

Here is one summary of the piece.Â  Here is a different, 2007 paper on the question.Â  Here is another related paper, and here (by Jagannathan and Sherman, much older draft, minus Jirnyi).Â  Here is a one-year-old ungated version of the main paper, I am not sure how much it differs.Â  Do any of you know of an ungated version of the current draft?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
This question has come up a few times lately in the blogosphere.Â  I've long found the market for such forecasts to beÂ a puzzling practice.Â  Sometimes the forecasts are purchased and other times they are given away, but either way money is being spent.Â 
The first question is whether those forecasts are more accurate than naive "random walk" models.Â  On average probably not, although you could argue thatÂ in a recession mean-reversion gives an edge to structuralÂ models.Â  Still, the forecasts are paid for in both good times and bad.Â  Note also that those who predicted our last crisis were, for the most part, giving that knowledge away for free.
Second, there are many such forecasts.Â  Even if some forecasts are quite useful, what's the value of supporting a marginal or additional forecast?Â  Is the next forecast to come along so much better?Â  Forecasts would seem to be the classic example of a public good.
I would explore other models.Â  Under one possibility, outsiders pay for the forecast to join a more exclusive club of clients with other privileges.Â  It's a bit like how art galleries won't sell their best pictures to complete outsiders but instead ask that you "pay your dues" by being a loyal customer for years.Â  In other words, it's an arbitrary fee to enforce price discrimination,Â backed by some plausible pretext.
Under a related model, the firm pays for the forecast as a means of generating publicity, signaling its size, seriousness, and audience, and in general marketing itself to outside clients.Â  It is unclear who bears the final incidence of these expenditures, the firm or the clients, but still "forecasting isn't about knowledge," as Robin Hanson would have said to the oracle at Delphi.
Either way, I do not put much credence in what the forecasts say.Â  They do usually represent "standard macroeconomic knowledge" and in that sense they are not a completeÂ fraud.Â  But the fact that they are being paid for does not, in my eyes, mean they are passing a market test in the traditional sense.
If anything, the persistence of the market in such forecasts should make you wonder about many of the other functions of these banks.
title: Why does anyone support private macroeconomic forecasts?

You can read his reply here.Â Â Note however that my criticisms explicitly are directed at narrow banking more generally, most of all my own (previous) version of the idea, not at the specific version ofÂ Kotlikoff's proposal.Â  There is one particular topic I did not deal with, and on it I will quoteÂ Kotlikoff reproducing my critique and responding to it:Â 

TC: A lot of what current banks do would be replicated by non-bank commercial lenders and the risk of the banking sector would be transferred somewhere else.Â 
LK: You missed the key point that all incorporated financial intermediaries have to operate as mutual fund companies. There are no â€œnon-bank commercial lendersâ€� unless they operate as proprietorships and partnerships and their owners have their houses and yachts on the line. The risk of the banking sector is reduced because we set it up to eliminate any chance of bank runs and gambling by the banks with the taxpayersâ€™ chips. Recall, the mutual funds are 100 percent equity financed at all times and in all situations.Â 
TC: Ideally, these non-bank lenders would engage in greater â€œmaturity-matching,â€� but if banks will exploit the moral hazard problem wonâ€™t these lenders exploit it too?Â Â 
LK: The only financial intermediaries who can operate under Limited Purpose Banking according to the current rules of the road are private banks with no limited liability.Â The lack of limited liability will eliminate the moral hazard problem.Â 

I am not inclined toÂ see unlimited liabilityÂ as a practical alternative.Â  How many businesses supply commercial credit?Â  Trade credit?Â  Credit by any other name? â€” namely contracts involving derivatives, annuities, insurance, repurchase agreements, etc., with intertemporal payments and embedded interest rates in the prices.Â  Would they allÂ have to give up limited liability?Â  Or would we end up channeling more financial intermediation through indirect credit transactions, while maintaining limited liability?Â  A version of thisÂ dilemmaÂ is experienced regularly by systems of equity-based Islamic banking..
Second, unlimited liability creates a pecuniary externality across shareholders.Â Â Who wants to be the remaining "fat cat" shareholder?Â  Why should Bill Gates ever invest?Â  Non-mutual fund banksÂ willÂ end up owned by thinly capitalized individuals or entities, thereby defeating the purpose of unlimited liability while at the same time raising transactions costs.Â  Walter Bagehot made this point, see also Joseph Grundfest, here is Hansmann and Kraakman with a reply.Â  Alex very ably surveys the main arguments in an MR post.
Unlimited liability is fineÂ for small-scale, private banking, especially in the international sector where tax evasion is a motive and the banks aren't fully part of any standard regulatory network.Â Â It doesn't work to force it on such a large sector of the economy as most commercial credit and non-bank lending.
In sum, I do not believe that narrow banking proposals benefit from being bundled with unlimited liability for other lenders.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
I have thoughtÂ about this question and now I seeÂ a new paper (ungated here) on the topic:

Genes and culture are often thought of as opposite ends of the natureâ€“nurture spectrum, but here we examine possible interactions. Genetic association studies suggest that variation within the genes of central neurotransmitter systems, particularly the serotonin (5-HTTLPR, MAOA-uVNTR) and opioid (OPRM1 A118G), are associated with individual differences in social sensitivity, which reflects the degree of emotional responsivity to social events and experiences. Here, we review recent work that has demonstrated a robust cross-national correlation between the relative frequency of variants in these genes and the relative degree of individualismâ€“collectivism in each population, suggesting that collectivism may have developed and persisted in populations with a high proportion of putative social sensitivity alleles because it was more compatible with such groups. Consistent with this notion, there was a correlation between the relative proportion of these alleles and lifetime prevalence of major depression across nations. The relationship between allele frequency and depression was partially mediated by individualismâ€“collectivism, suggesting that reduced levels of depression in populations with a high proportion of social sensitivity alleles is due to greater collectivism. These results indicate that genetic variation may interact with ecological and social factors to influence psychocultural differences. 

Still,Â I can'tÂ see the evidence.Â Â I don't see the caseÂ for causation.Â  Let's say something about a group's serotonin level made it more susceptible to social stress: couldn't that lead to either greater individualism or greater collectivism?Â  Is collectivism so calming and are social institutions so functional so as to respond to how stressed we feel from social interactions?Â  If I were a very stressed out person (I'm not), wouldn't I prefer to live in or construct the social institutions of Sweden, which in this context counts as individualistic?Â  
You might respond that the evolving allelesÂ should be linked toÂ earlier Swedish society and not Sweden today.Â  ButÂ then one needs to measure collectivism vs. individualism at that earlier point in time.Â  I wouldn't be surprised if China in the tenth century were "more individualistic" than Sweden in the age of the Vikings, and so on.
(By the way, Is "individualism vs. collectivism" the right spectrum?Â  We individualistic Americans seem especially apt at being trained to kill people and fire when ordered.Â  We also seem especially patriotic.)
If you pull out the strangely-placed Colombia from Figure 1 in the paper, it's basically a Europeans vs. Asians effect driving both the genetic contrasts and the collectivism vs. individualism contrasts.Â  We'reÂ left with two quite general contrasts and no theory connecting the two or much of a goodÂ reason to think they should be connected.
Don't we just have two data points here â€” "Asia" and "Europe" â€” and the split of the data into countries is a phony way to boost apparent statistical significance?
It's a broader question what effects higher serotonin levels have.Â  I've tried to read a few papers on this topic and I've seen high serotonin levels correlated with both anxiety and calm.Â  To be sure, this may reflect the inability of this non-specialist to see through to the best and best understood results, but still the relevance of serotonin to human behaviorÂ hardly seems like an open and shut question.Â  I'd sooner suggest that right now we don't understand serotonin very well, at least not as it shapes broader social interactions.
I thank RR for the relevant pointer.
title: Is there a genetic component to varying degrees of cooperativeness?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
I've been having discussions with someÂ associates about what it means when a measured short-run multiplier is positive yet less than one.Â  It is occasionallyÂ suggested that a multiplier less than one means that fiscal policy is necessarily a bad idea, but I don't see it that way.Â 
Keep in mind there is no a priori argumentÂ that the government purchases "don't count," even though sometimes they don't produce much value ex post.Â  And the borrowed dollar isn't "taken out" of the economy in a meaningful way.Â  It can comeÂ from abroad or it can accelerate velocity, at least potentially.
Let's say the multiplier is 1.0.Â  That typically means a dollar is spent on a road (or whatever), which is in the plus one column.Â  There is some crowding out of private investment but not usually one hundred percent.Â  Let's say that's minus 30 cents.Â  The spending on the road, and road workers, has some positive second-order effects.Â  Let's say those are plus thirty cents per dollar.
In that particular case, the multiplier ends up as equal to one and that is net, all things considered.Â Â The spending still would yieldÂ a short-term positive for gdp if the multiplier were 0.5.
The case against fiscal policy should examineÂ long-term budgetary costs, possible confidence factors,Â implementation lags, political economy problems, difficulties in targeting unemployed resources, and also the (underrated) notion that sometimes fiscal policy postpones problems into the medium run rather than solving them through jump-starting a recovery.Â  But it is difficult to deny that fiscal policy brings some economic benefits in the short run, or can brake an economic decline, even if the measured multiplier is less than one or for that matter well under one.Â Â 
As an aside, IÂ do notÂ prefer to emphasizeÂ the notion of "investment crowding out" for analyzingÂ fiscal policy.Â  The notion is a coherent one, but frequently analysts, and audiences,Â end up confusing nominal flows of finance with real resource opportunity costs.Â  I instead prefer to askÂ how effectively the fiscal policy is targeting real unemployed resources and to deemphasizeÂ the financial angle, at leastÂ for the first-order analysis.
title: Confusions about the multiplier < 1 (me defending fiscal policy, sort of)

Bryan Caplan asks:

Is anyone willing to often even a semi-plausible economic argument in defense of mandatory national origin labels?

I oppose the policy, but the obvious argument in favor is that the practice canÂ partially cartelize consumers and oppose market power.Â  The label, if it discouragesÂ some customers at the margin, could induce lower prices and higher quantity (and quality)Â from the foreign firms with market power.Â Â 
In opposition, IÂ would note that many of these markets (e.g., textiles) are quite competitive or that sometimes labels will boost the market powerÂ of the producers who are not discriminatedÂ against.Â  Or if the label means some customers won't buy the foreign product no matter what, it could beÂ the inelastic customers are left in the market and pricesÂ go up.Â Â Ethically speaking, the whole idea rubs me the wrong way, as it does Bryan.
Without any law, the "desired" countries and regions of origin will add a label voluntarily, and consumers will make inferences against non-labeled products, thus offeringÂ most of theÂ benefitsÂ a coerciveÂ policy might bring.

author: Alex Tabarrok
text:
Ted Frank reports on his 60k weight-loss bet with Ray Lehmann:
In late 2008, Ray Lehmann and I made an audacious bet: we would put up $60,000 that we would lose 60 pounds in nine months, and pay each other $1,000 for each pound the other lost.Â 


â€¦I lost 32 pounds, Ray lost 41, and we were on pace to lose 60 each. StickK.com was offering to make us their official spokespeople. 


Then things fell apart. We couldn't negotiate an appropriate contract with StickK, which wanted exclusive rights to our story without any compensation. The delay caused us to stop writing about the diet while we had false dreams of fame and glory from StickK promotion, and then we both got distracted with starting new jobs and the disappointment of shattered expectations when StickK stopped returning our calls.



Alex Tabarrok correctly predicted that the danger of the two-person bet was that we would collude not to enforce it.


And, indeed that was what happened. We started gaining weight, and started pushing back the goal-line for the end of the betâ€¦neither of us held the other's feet to the fireâ€¦.


Professor Tabarrok's solution was to create a third-party Leviathan to enforce the bet: he facetiously offered to pay us $500 to be the collectorÂ [not facetious, Ted!, AT]. Of course, that was a negative-expectation transaction for each of us, unless we thought we had a 90%+ chance of succeedingâ€¦Even the threat of public humiliation on Marginal Revolution wasn't enough to stop us from colluding.

But Ted isn't giving up. Â He is looking for other people to take the bet to reduce the possibility of collusion or he would like to auction off leviathan rights.
Are there three other people out there willing to wager that they can lose 50 pounds over a reasonable amount of time? (Forty? Sixty?) Who's in, and under what conditions?
â€¦In the alternative, how much is someone willing to pay to be Leviathan and have the opportunity to collect tens of thousands of dollars from me or Ray for failing to lose weight? I suppose I could put Leviathan rights up on eBay; if Marginal Revolution and a few other blogs publicized it, we could reach a good solid equilibrium price. What do people think?

I see this is as a good case study in the difficult of setting up an appropriate incentive scheme and also the difficulty of losing weight. When I put on my Tyler hat, however, I have to wonder whether all this effort put into clever incentive schemes is not a way of avoiding the real issues. Â "Less blogging, more jogging," my friends.
What Ted and Ray are trying to do is to sail between Scylla and Charybdis by offsetting the pull of food with the pull of lost money. Carrot cake versus stick. But in this tug of war, how long will the balance last? How permanent will the weight loss be?
The real trick in weight loss, as in other areas of life, is to change wants not oppose them. Unfortunately,Â Seth Roberts nothwithstanding, this is a struggle with no easy solutions.
Nevertheless, I have proudly helpedÂ others to lose weight with unusual incentives,Â and my $500 bid for leviathan rights over Ted and Ray still stands. Good luck guys.
title: Weight Loss and Incentives

Hereâ€™s a video of a small town in Britain that turned its traffic lights off. Â Order ensued.

The experiment is not unique. Tom Vanderbilt wrote an excellent piece in The Wilson Quarterly a few years ago on traffic revolutionary Hans Monderman (see also this NYTimes piece) who has redesigned a number of city centers:

	At the town center, in a crowded four-way intersection called the Laweiplein, Monderman removed not only the traffic lights but virtually every other traffic control. Instead of a space cluttered with poles, lights, â€œtraffic islands,â€� and restrictive arrows, Monderman installed a radical kind of roundabout (a â€œsquareabout,â€� in his words, because it really seemed more a town square than a traditional roundabout), marked only by a raised circle of grass in the middle, several fountains, and some very discreet indicators of the direction of traffic, which were required by law.


	As I watched the intricate social ballet that occurred as cars and bikes slowed to enter the circle (pedestrians were meant to cross at crosswalks placed a bit before the intersection), Monderman performed a favorite trick. He walked, backward and with eyes closed, into the Laweiplein. The traffic made its way around him. No one honked, he wasnâ€™t struck. Instead of a binary, mechanistic processâ€“stop, goâ€“the movement of traffic and pedestrians in the circle felt human and organic.


	A year after the change, the results of this â€œextreme makeoverâ€� were striking: Not only had congestion decreased in the intersectionâ€“buses spent less time waiting to get through, for exampleâ€“but there were half as many accidents, even though total car traffic was up by a third.
The experiments are interesting in their own right but they are also very good illustrations of spontaneous order; how order is possible without orders.
Hat tip: Dan Klein.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
David Leonhardt has a very good piece which presentsÂ some relevant facts about unemployment.Â  Felix Salmon summarizes one part of the pieceÂ as follows:

In 2008, only 13.2% of the labor force was unemployed at some point. That compares to 18.1% in 1980, and 22% in 1982.


Real wages, which normally fall during recessions, have risen in this one. Even nominal wages are up. 

Also from Felix:

The overriding impression is of most Americans actually doing OK, with an unemployable underclass bearing the brunt of the recession.

To those observationsÂ I would add that corporate profits are doing fairly well.
Those facts, in a nutshell, are why I am not AD-obsessed when it comes to explaining the current economy.Â  
Furthermore, I don't buy the idea thatÂ so manyÂ of the unemployed are stupidly and stubbornly holding out for a higher wage than they can get, while at the same time they can be reemployed by a mere bit of money illusion.Â  There are so many blog posts written to the Fed, to Bernanke, etc. "Hey guys, goose up the money supply!Â  Bernanke, read your old writings!"Â  
Yet I have seen not one such post to the unemployed: "Hey guys, lower your wage demands!Â  It's good for you!Â  You'll get a job and avoid the soul-sucking ravages of idleness.Â  It's good for the country!Â  It's good for Bernanke, you'll get those regional Fed presidents off his back!Â  Why not?Â  The best you can hope for is to get tricked by money illusion anyway!Â  Show up those elites and get to that equilibrium on your own!Â  Take control!" and so on.Â  If such posts would seem patently absurd, we should ask what that implies for our underlyingÂ theory of current unemployment.
I sooner think of these unemployed individuals as having gone down economic corridors which are no longer promising and not facing any easy adjustment to set things right again.Â Â FurthermoreÂ I consider that portrait of their troubles to beÂ more consistent with the general tenor of liberal, left-wing, and progressive thought, not to mention plain common sense.
Elsewhere, Matt Yglesias has anÂ interesting post on the recalculation argument and its relation to political ideology.Â  He claims that promoting the argument will make people like capitalism less and that may well be true.Â  I would add:
1. The Industrial Revolution also was a tough slog for quite a few decades.Â  Yet it was both worthwhile and it gave capitalism a bad name forÂ a longÂ time.
2. Alexander Field argues that the Great Depression brought greater productivity improvements than any other decade in U.S. history.
3. If one wishes to consider state intervention, in light of recalculation, one is pointed in the direction of direct employment of the struggling workers; the recalculation argument does not rule out interventionÂ per se.Â  This advice could potentially beÂ useful and I don't see why even libertarians shouldÂ consider it necessarily worse than $800 billion of fiscal stimulus.
4. Like Matt and many others, I favor a more expansionary monetary policy.Â  But the last stimulus was oversold and there is no reason to oversell this one.Â  We really don't know how well it will work (and I'm not referring to liquidity traps).Â  But if the Fed tries more monetary expansion, we'll see how much of the current employment is cyclical and AD-related in the traditional sense.
5. By its very nature, a recalculation argument ought to be somewhat agnostic as to how much (and what kind) of recalculation is actually required.Â  See #4.
Addendum: Bryan Caplan comments, non-ironically.

author: Alex Tabarrok
text:
From David Foster Wallace's 1995 essay, The String Theory: 
â€¦ it's better for us not to know the kinds of sacrifices the professional-grade athlete has made to get so very good at one particular thing. Oh, we'll invoke lush cliches about the lonely heroism of Olympic athletes, the pain and analgesia of football, the early rising and hours of practice and restricted diets, the preflight celibacy, et cetera. But the actual facts of the sacrifices repel us when we see them: basketball geniuses who cannot read, sprinters who dope themselves, defensive tackles who shoot up with bovine hormones until they collapse or explode. We prefer not to consider closely the shockingly vapid and primitive comments uttered by athletes in postcontest interviews or to consider what impoverishments in one's mental life would allow people actually to think the way great athletes seem to think. Note the way "up close and personal" profiles of professional athletes strain so hard to find evidence of a rounded human life â€” outside interests and activities, values beyond the sport. We ignore what's obvious, that most of this straining is farce. It's farce because the realities of top-level athletics today require an early and total commitment to one area of excellence. An ascetic focus. A subsumption of almost all other features of human life to one chosen talent and pursuit. A consent to live in a world that, like a child's world, is very small. 

Hat tip to Tim Carmody filling in at Kottke.

I haven't followed the numerical specifics of his plan (see Krugman, McArdle, and Ezra), which will never be voted on, so at this pointÂ I'm more interested in the general problem motivatingÂ the reform.Â  We all know that health care spending has to be restrained in some manner.Â  There are (at least) two approaches:
1. Have the federal government take a more active role in shutting down or limiting some reimbursements, based on efficacy studiesÂ ("death panels").
2. Turn some or all of Medicare into a fixed voucher program and let individualsÂ choose which set of restrictions they will accept from private suppliers ("grandma bangs on HMO door").
As I understand Ryan's approach, he is putting a great deal of emphasis on #2, whereas most Democrats favorÂ #1.
Which mix of #1 and #2 is best is one question; which mix people will accept politically is another.Â  A third issueÂ is which mix is time consistent and a fourth is which prevents "rationed" people from simply popping up somewhere else in the public health system.Â  I would start with those distinctions and see which policy direction people need to be nudged in, relative to the path we are on now.Â  That probably means greater acceptance of both #1 and #2, to some extent.
I believeÂ that #2 works fine for a lot of health care, especially the less controversial and less emotional areas of care,Â such asÂ laser eye surgery.Â  Neither #1 nor #2 work especially well, or are especially popular, for end of life issues.
Whatever problems the Ryan plan may have (should we dismiss all ideas from people with overly optimistic forecasts?), I take his contribution to be a nudge in the direction of #2, given the current political equilibrium.Â  Overall I see this as a healthy nudge, even if you think that relying fully or even mainly on #2 isÂ undesirable, infeasible, and time inconsistent.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Pete Boettke says "policy is the problem."Â  Ezra says he can't find evidence that policy is the problem.
I hold the intermediate view that policy uncertaintyÂ is a problem but not the problem.Â  On one hand, policy uncertainty probably has been greatest for the health care sector, yet job growth in that sector has been relatively robust.Â  Furthermore, Obamacare may bring uncertainty, but part of the uncertainty is about whether employers can get away with dumping their workers onto the subsidized exchanges.Â  Arguably that should help hiring rather than hurt it.
I expect electoral gridlock by November yet no one seems to be welcoming that "certainty" very much.
Perhaps most importantly, deleveraging recessions usually take a long time to recover from in any case and there's not a lot of good cheer along the way.
I would be more convinced by the uncertainty view if it were combined into a larger, coherent story, consistent with reported corporate profits being fairly high.
Do the implicit volatilities embedded in option prices show a lot of expected uncertainty?Â  Maybe, but again I'm waiting to see the evidence.Â  If so, this one should be staring us right in the face.
On the other side of the ledger, the tax code remains highly uncertain, to our detriment,Â and monetary policy isÂ some mix of uncertain and baffling (though see the above point on implicit volatilities).Â  
ThereÂ is also behavioral economics.Â  An image or speech or proposed law can crush a mood, whether or not that is rational.Â  I can't cite a lot of systematicÂ evidence for this having happened, but I knowÂ from talking to people how many of them think, rightly or wrongly, that Obama is very very bad for the American economy.Â  I believe that is a factor in our slow recovery.Â  
Be careful to separate your positive and normative views here.Â  Maybe the audience is "at fault," rather than the messenger, but still some people are veryÂ upset.Â  Every time I read a left-wingÂ writer dismantling "right-wing media" I think they are actually providing another data point for the policy uncertainty hypothesis, although that is hardly their intent.Â Â In many circles there is a perceived problem with our country, regardless how much thatÂ is based on fact or not.Â  If food consumers can be irrational and moody, political consumers (who are also investors) can be the same.Â  Still, I don't know how significant this factor is.
Temporary hiring is quite high, while permanent hiring is not.Â  However that need not show that the decisiveÂ uncertainty comes from politics.Â  Furthermore itÂ instead could mean that the fixed cost of hiring labor full-time is high but not uncertain.
A lot of the current uncertainty is about a higher estimate of overall systemic risk, rather than from politics per se.Â  Such risk worries may be a blend of private and public sector factors, such as worries about Europe or China.Â Â Economic and political uncertainty are not always separable categories.
Overall I don't seeÂ a lot ofÂ clear evidence on thisÂ question but I thinkÂ policy uncertaintyÂ is one factor, albeit an exaggerated factor in many circles.
title: Is policy uncertainty the problem?

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Here is my latest NYT column, for the ideas I am indebted to pointers from Daniel Klein, Matt Yglesias, and of course Donald Shoup.
Here is the bottom line:

If developers were allowed to face directly the high land costs of providing so much parking, the number of spaces would be a result of a careful economic calculation rather than a matter of satisfying a legal requirement. Parking would be scarcer, and more likely to have a price â€“ or a higher one than it does now â€“ and people would be more careful about when and where they drove. 
The subsidies are largely invisible to drivers who park their cars â€“ and thus free or cheap parking spaces feel like natural outcomes of the market, or perhaps even an entitlement. Yet the law is allocating this land rather than letting market prices adjudicate whether we need more parking, and whether that parking should be free. We end up overusing land for cars â€“ and overusing cars too. You donâ€™t have to hate sprawl, or automobiles, to want to stop subsidizing that way of life. 

Here are a few quotations from the article:

â€œMinimum parking requirements act like a fertility drug for cars.â€� 

And:

As Professor Shoup puts it: â€œWho pays for free parking? Everyone but the motorist.â€� 

And:

If we donâ€™t give away cars, why give away parking spaces?

What are the biggest problems with the idea?Â  First, the danger of spillover parking means that a lot of parking has to be properly priced all at once.Â  If the local K-Mart has a smaller lot, you don't want the customers flooding a neighborhood street and simply shifting the problem.Â  The proper correction requires a coordinated pricing and enforcement effort, not only to succeed, but also to be sufficiently popular with homeowners.Â  Fortunately, most of the coordination can be done at the level of the individual town or city.
Second, we don't yet know how many more spaces would be priced in the absence of legalÂ minimum parking requirements, andÂ how many fewer car trips there would be, especially if we are holding the quantity and quality of mass transit constant.Â  The employer still may wish to subsidize appearance at the workplace.Â  Alternatively, "parking fees as lump sum tax" is fine by me and it bears an odd but pleasant connection to Georgist ideas.Â Â Another possibility is that a lot of parking is shifted to satellite lots, combined with small buses or shuttles; Tysons Corner Mall already does this at Christmas or consider any number of airports.Â  ThatÂ still would improve land use (and welfare), but it remains an open question how much congestionÂ and emissions would get better.
Mark Thoma discusses some distributional issues.Â  I would note that less land for parking should lower other real estate and retail prices, even if more poor people end up taking the bus.Â  And the very poorest Americans often don't have cars at all.

Which country's stock market has been the best performer in the world â€” not just over the past year or decade, but over the last 110 years? 
It's Australia, which stands above all others in its combination of higher returns and lower volatility. 
While they speak our language, and we have some common origins, they have hitched their wagon to the dynamic growth of Asia. And it's paid off, as Australia has had the best performing stock market in the world from 1900 to 2009. 
Australia posted 7.5% after-inflation returns per year during that time, with a standard deviation of 18.2%, according to a study from Credit Suisse. Those returns are the highest and the volatility the second lowest of the 19 major markets the researchers studied.
During that time, U.S. stocks made a 6.2% return, with a standard deviation of 20.4%. That means investors would have made more money in Australian stocks with less volatility than in the U.S. or any other major market over that long stretch.

text:
W. Bowman Cutter, Sofia F. Franco, and Autumn DeWoody have a new paper titledÂ "Do Minimum Parking Requirements Force Developers to Provide More Parking than Privately Optimal?"Â The abstract is this:

Minimum parking requirements are the norm for urban and suburban development in the United States (Davidson and Dolnick (2002)). The justification for parking space requirements is that overflow parking will occupy nearby street or off-street parking. Shoup (1999) and Willson (1995) provides cases where there is reason to believe that parking space requirements have forced parcel developers to place more parking than they would in the absence of parking requirements. If the effect of parking minimums is to significantly increase the land area devoted to parking, then the increase in impervious surfaces would likely cause water quality degradation, increased flooding, and decreased groundwater recharge. However, to our knowledge the existing literature does not test the effect of parking minimums on the amount of lot space devoted to parking beyond a few case studies. This paper tests the hypothesis that parking space requirements cause an oversupply of parking by examining the implicit marginal value of land allocated to parking spaces. This is an indirect test of the effects of parking requirements that is similar to Glaeser and Gyourko (2003). A simple theoretical model shows that the marginal value of additional parking to the sale price should be equal to the cost of land plus the cost of parking construction. We estimate the marginal values of parking and lot area with spatial methods using a large data set from the Los Angeles area non-residential property sales and find that for most of the property types the marginal value of parking is significantly below that of the parcel area. This evidence supports the contention that minimum parking requirements significantly increase the amount of parcel area devoted to parking.

Well, more or less.Â  Or is it an iPad?Â  In 1910 StossÂ published an essay called "The Wireless Century," intending to predict the world of 2010.Â  In this world everyone carries around a "wireless telegraph" which:
1. Serves as a telephone, the whole world over.

4. Can allow people to send each other photographs, across the entire world.
5. Can allow people to see the images of paintings, museums, etc. in distant locales.
6. No one will ever be alone again.Â  
7. Can serve as a means of payment, connecting people to their bank accounts and enabling payments (Japan is ahead of us here).
8. CanÂ connect people to all newspapers, although Sloss predicted that people would prefer that the device read the paper aloud to them (not so much the case).

10. People will have a better sense of the poor, and of suffering, because they will have witnessed it through their device (not obviously true, at least not yet).

14.Â Married couples will be much closer, andÂ distance relationships will be closer and better.

author: Tyler Cowen
text:
Arnold isn't convinced:

If we abolished free parking, would parking spaces be scarcer? Keep in mind that if the price of parking went up, this would cause movement along the supply curve as well as along the demand curve. Maybe the total number of parking places would decline (it depends on elasticities), but the one result you can predict with certainty is that the number of unused parking places would go up. Is that necessarily welfare-improving?

The key is not to "abolish" free parking, but to a) abolish minimum parking requirements, and b) putÂ prices or higher prices on congestedÂ municipal-owned parking spaces.Â  Both a) and b) will lower the demand for parking and a) will lower the supply of parking, so why should the number of unused parking spaces necessarily go up?Â  If you treat something as an appropriately scarce resource, it should be used more effectively.
There are plenty of DC restaurants which don't have their own parking lots, but they use paid valet parking and findÂ ingenious ways to store carsÂ more effectively.Â  The parking fee means that some people walk there or use the Metro, rather than driving and parking.Â  No one finds this arrangement especially objectionable and while valet parking is at a discount to marketÂ still it is priced.Â  At lunch time valet parking is less likely but still people pay to park, usually in nearby lots.Â  No one wouldÂ suggest that these restaurants be forced to put in minimum parking.Â Â Nor would anyone suggest that mandated minimums would be neutral with respect to parking efficiency.
I'm simply asking for the same switch in reverse, namely to do away with minimum parking requirements.Â  Very likely,Â such a changeÂ will have a bigger impact on future developments than on past developments (it can be hard to reconfigure a parking lot), although some malls might sell off or rent their now-liberated parking spots to other commercial ventures.
Pricing parking on busy residential streets is just common sense S&D and the price should vary with peak times.
Most of all, I am calling for "parking recalculation," so I am surprised Arnold is skeptical.Â Â Maybe he thinks the recalculation won't bring much change (the Wal-Mart in North Dakota may never charge for parking), but in fact we find a wide variety of parking pricing practices around the world and even around the U.S., as laws and institutions and real net prices vary.
You could argue that politics already pushes us to somewhat efficient outcomes for policy, as indeed NYC does usually (though not always) treat parking spaces as more scarce than does Fargo, North Dakota.Â  Still, there is an obvious chain for political failure.Â  Development decisions are very often made on a one-by-one, sequential basis.Â  Other merchants, or nearby homeowners, fear parking overflow and they lobby as if this private cost were actually a social cost.Â  At each step of development, lots of parties are pushing for minimum parking requirements.Â  Some "once-and-for-all" parking policy decisions could limit this political incentive.Â  
Another simple public choice story is this: minimum parking limits the supply of land and boosts the returns to local homeowners.Â  It raises retail prices but many of the store's customers are from out of town, so that is a vote-winning strategy at the local level, namely scarcer land and higher prices for stores.
People who drive cars also have disproportionately more political power than people who do not, especially in most suburban areas.
Most of the time, legal quantity minimums have real effects on markets and they are not set efficiently at the political level.
Addendum: Here is Arnold's response to Robin, here is Robin on Arnold.Â Â And yet more from Arnold.Â  And here is an O'Toole comment; for one thing there is free parking in Manhattan, but for anotherâ€¦I never claimed there was.
From the comments: "A note of clarification about free parking in Manhattan. By law meters are prohibited on residential streets. Only on commercial streets and corners are meters allowed. Residential parking permits are also prohibited by the state. This means that in many parts of the island (mostly above 59th street though also in certain areas of lower Manhattan) there is "free" parking at the curb. In these neighborhoods there is substantial cruising for parking. In addition, all of Manhattan was subject to minimum parking requirements until 1982, and now areas north of Central Park (roughly) are subject to minimum parking requirements, as are the other boroughs."

Dust is the lunar astronaut's nemesis.Â  With no water or wind to smooth them, the tiny, hard moon rock particles remain sharp.Â  They scratched faceplates and camera lenses during Apollo, destroyed bearings, clogged equipment joints.Â  Dusting on the moon is a fool's errand.Â  Unlike on the Earth, where the planet's magnetic field wards off charged particles of solar wind, these particles bombard the moon's surface and impart an electrostatic charge.Â  Moon dust clings like dryer socks.Â  Astronauts who stepped from the Lunar Module in gleaming white marshamllow suits returned a few hours later looking like miners.Â  The Apollo 12 suits and long johns became so filthy that at one point, astronaut Jim Lovell told me, the crew "took off all their underwear and they were naked for half the way home."

I am outsourcing this post entirely to Matt Yglesias because it's awesome and it made me very happy to see how public choice has moved out in the world:
A number of people, including many commenters here and even alleged
conservative James Joyner think you should need a professional license to become
a barber because you might hurt
someone with a straight razor. Uh huh. At best this would be an argument for
regulating people who do shaves with a straight razor, which would be
considerably narrower than current comprehensive regulation of hair
stylists.
Meanwhile, though â€œtorts and the free market will take care of itâ€� isnâ€™t the
answer to everything, itâ€™s surely the answer to some things. Getting
some kind of training before you shave a dude with a straight razor is obviously
desirable in terms of strict self-interest. If you screw it up in a serious way,
youâ€™ll face serious personal consequences and the only way to make money doing
itâ€“and weâ€™re talking about a very modest sum of moneyâ€“is to do it properly.
People also ought to try to think twice about whether their views are being
driven by pure status quo bias. Barbers are totally unregulated in
the United Kingdom, is there some social crisis resulting
from this? Barber regulations differ from state to state, are the stricter
states experiencing some kind of important public health gains?
Last you really do need to look at how these things play out in practice. If
you just assume optimal implementation of regulation, then regulation always
looks good. But as I noted
in the initial post the way this works in practice is the boards are
dominated by incumbent practitioners looking to limit supply. One result is that
in Michigan (and perhaps elsewhere) itâ€™s hard for
ex-convicts to get barber licenses which harms the public interest not only
by raising the cost of haircuts, but by preventing people from making a
legitimate living. States generally donâ€™t grant reciprocity to other statesâ€™
licensing boards, which limits supply even though no rational person worries
about state-to-state variance in barber licensing when they move to a New Place.
In New Jersey, you need to take the
straight razor shaving test to cut womenâ€™s hair because theyâ€™re thinking up
arbitrary ways to incrementally raise the barrier to entry.
In principle, you could deal with all these problems piecemeal. But
realistically this sort of problem is inevitably going to arise when you pit the
concentrated interest of incumbent haircutters against the diffuse interest of
consumers. Itâ€™s hard enough to make sure that really important regulatory
functions related to environmental protection, public safety, and financial
stability are done properly.
